title: Fall Protection — General Requirements
talking_points: In construction, fall protection is required at 6 feet above a lower level — in general industry, the trigger is 4 feet. Know which standard applies to your task today.
Acceptable fall protection systems include guardrails, safety nets, and personal fall arrest systems (PFAS). Your supervisor will determine which system fits the task.
Guardrail top rails must be 42 inches high (plus or minus 3 inches) and withstand 200 pounds of outward or downward force without failure.
Floor holes and wall openings must be covered or guarded. Covers must support at least twice the maximum intended load and be marked 'HOLE' or 'COVER.'
Never remove or disable fall protection — if you find a guardrail missing or a hole cover displaced, stop work, secure the area, and notify your supervisor immediately.
discussion_prompt: What's one area on this jobsite right now where you think fall protection could be improved — and what would you do about it?

title: Ladder Safety — Portable Ladders
talking_points: Inspect all rungs and rails before use — set aside any ladder with cracks, loose hardware, bent rails, or missing feet.
Set the base 1 foot out for every 4 feet of height. Secure the top against the structure so it cannot slide or shift.
Maintain three points of contact at all times — two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand.
Never stand on the top two rungs of a stepladder or the top three rungs of an extension ladder.
Face the ladder when climbing — do not lean or reach beyond the side rails. Move the ladder instead of overreaching.
discussion_prompt: If you get to a ladder and notice a bent rung, what do you do — and who do you tell?

title: Ladder Safety — Fixed Ladders
talking_points: Fixed ladders taller than 24 feet must have a ladder safety system or personal fall arrest system — cages alone no longer meet the standard for new installations.
OSHA is phasing out existing cage and well systems by November 2036. If your site still has caged ladders, know that a retrofit is coming.
Before climbing a fixed ladder, check the rungs for corrosion, ice, grease, or damage. Report any deficiencies before use.
Use the ladder safety system properly — attach the sleeve or connector to your harness D-ring before you begin climbing and do not detach until you reach a safe platform.
At the top and bottom of fixed ladders, there should be a clear landing platform. Never step off a ladder into an unprotected area.
discussion_prompt: Have you ever climbed a fixed ladder that didn't feel safe? What was wrong with it, and what did you do?

title: Scaffolding — Supported Scaffolds
talking_points: Every scaffold must support its own weight plus at least four times the maximum intended load without failure.
Fall protection is required when the scaffold platform is 10 feet or more above the ground — this means guardrails, PFAS, or both depending on the scaffold type.
Scaffold planks must be scaffold-grade lumber or manufactured decking. The gap between the platform and the face of the work must not exceed 14 inches (10 inches for plastering and lathing).
Mudsills and base plates are required. Never build a scaffold on unstable ground — bricks, blocks, or barrels are not acceptable as a foundation.
Toeboards at least 3.5 inches high are required along open edges to prevent tools and materials from falling onto workers below.
discussion_prompt: What's the first thing you check before stepping onto a scaffold at the start of your shift?

title: Scaffolding — Suspended Scaffolds
talking_points: Suspension ropes must support six times the intended load — this is a higher safety factor than supported scaffolds because the consequences of rope failure are catastrophic.
Every worker on a suspended scaffold must wear a full-body harness attached to an independent lifeline — the scaffold guardrails alone are not sufficient.
Inspect wire ropes daily for broken wires, kinking, corrosion, and bird-caging. Remove any rope that shows damage.
Counterweights must be non-flowable (no sand or water) and secured to the outrigger beam — do not use construction materials that may be removed during the project.
Before use each day, test the hoist by raising the platform 12 inches and confirming the brakes hold. If the platform drifts, do not use the scaffold.
discussion_prompt: Why do you think suspended scaffolds require a higher safety factor than supported scaffolds?

title: Scaffolding — Access and Erection
talking_points: Safe access — a ladder, stair tower, or ramp — is required whenever the scaffold platform is more than 2 feet above or below a point of access.
Climbing on cross-braces is prohibited. If there is no built-in ladder or stair, one must be provided before anyone works on the scaffold.
Only a competent person may direct the erection, moving, dismantling, or alteration of a scaffold. If you are not that person, do not modify the scaffold.
During erection and dismantling, fall protection is still required for workers at height — this is when many scaffold-related injuries occur.
Tag scaffolds clearly: green tag means fully inspected and safe; red tag means incomplete or unsafe — never use a red-tagged scaffold.
discussion_prompt: What would you do if you saw someone climbing the cross-braces to reach a scaffold platform?

title: Aerial Lifts and Scissor Lifts
talking_points: In a boom lift (articulating or telescoping), a full-body harness with a lanyard attached to the basket is required at all times — do not tie off to an adjacent structure.
In a scissor lift, the guardrail system is the primary fall protection. A harness is generally not required unless the manufacturer or site rules say otherwise.
Perform a ground-level inspection before each use: check controls, hydraulics, outriggers, tires, and guardrails. Test all functions at ground level before elevating.
Never stand on the guardrails or use a ladder or step stool inside the basket to gain extra height.
Be aware of overhead hazards — power lines, structural steel, ceiling obstructions — and maintain safe clearances as you reposition.
discussion_prompt: Why do you think boom lifts require a harness but scissor lifts generally don't?

title: Leading Edge Work
talking_points: A leading edge is any unprotected side or edge of a floor, roof, or deck where work is actively in progress — fall protection is required at 6 feet.
Acceptable protection at a leading edge includes guardrails, safety nets, or PFAS. A controlled access zone is allowed only when conventional methods are infeasible.
If using PFAS at a leading edge, the maximum allowable freefall distance is 6 feet, and the system must limit arrest force to 1,800 pounds.
Controlled access zones must be at least 6 feet back from the edge and marked with a control line 39 to 45 inches high. Only authorized workers may enter.
Leading edge work is one of the most common situations for fatal falls. If your protection is missing or inadequate, stop work and speak up — it can save a life.
discussion_prompt: Have you ever worked near a leading edge where the fall protection felt inadequate? What would you do differently?

title: Roofing — Low-Slope Roofs
talking_points: On a low-slope roof in construction, a combination of a warning line and safety monitor is permitted in certain conditions — but PFAS or guardrails are always the safer choice.
Warning lines must be set back at least 6 feet from the roof edge, supported by stanchions, and flagged every 6 feet for visibility.
In general industry, the rules use a tiered approach: within 6 feet of the edge, conventional fall protection is required. Between 6 and 15 feet, a designated area may be used for infrequent work.
Roof openings and skylights are fall hazards too — they must be guarded or covered with materials that support twice the intended load.
Wind, rain, ice, and debris all increase fall risk on roofs. Evaluate conditions before starting work and reassess throughout the day.
discussion_prompt: What additional precautions do you think are needed when working on a roof in wet or windy conditions?

title: Roofing — Steep-Slope Roofs
talking_points: A steep-slope roof is any roof with a pitch greater than 4 inches of rise per 12 inches of run. Fall protection is required at 6 feet.
On steep-slope roofs, a safety monitor system alone is NOT permitted — you must use guardrails, safety nets, or PFAS.
Roof brackets (also called roof jacks) provide a temporary work platform and can serve as an anchor point when properly installed.
Footwear matters — wear boots with slip-resistant soles designed for roof work. Smooth-soled shoes are a leading contributor to roof falls.
Never walk on a steep roof without your fall protection attached. Even experienced roofers can lose footing — gravity does not care about your skill level.
discussion_prompt: What's the steepest roof you've worked on, and what fall protection was used?

title: Floor Openings, Holes, and Covers
talking_points: Any hole in a floor, roof, or walking surface large enough for a person to step into or fall through must be covered or guarded.
Covers must be strong enough to support at least twice the maximum intended load, including workers, equipment, and materials.
Covers must be secured so they cannot be accidentally displaced — nail them, screw them, or bolt them in place.
Mark all covers clearly with the word 'HOLE' or 'COVER' in a contrasting color so no one mistakes them for part of the floor.
If you see a cover that has been removed or displaced, do not walk past it. Secure the area, replace the cover, and report it.
discussion_prompt: Why do you think displaced or unmarked hole covers are such a common cause of falls?

title: Steel Erection — Fall Protection
talking_points: Connectors (ironworkers making initial connections) are exempt from fall protection below 15 feet, but must be protected above 30 feet for decking operations.
Between 15 and 30 feet, connectors must have completed connector training and be provided with a PFAS, even if they choose when to use it.
Controlled decking zones are permitted for initial decking of steel structures — these zones have specific size limits and must be clearly marked.
At least two bolts must be installed at each connection point before the load is released from the crane. This is the minimum for structural integrity.
A site-specific erection plan is required and must address fall protection, crane procedures, and the sequence of steel placement.
discussion_prompt: Why do you think ironworkers have different fall protection height triggers than other trades?

title: Stairways and Handrails
talking_points: A handrail is required on stairways with four or more risers, or where the stairway rises more than 30 inches.
Handrail height must be between 30 and 37 inches measured from the leading edge of the stair tread to the top of the rail.
Stair treads must be at least 4 inches deep (for pan-type treads filled to the top), and risers must be between 6.5 and 12 inches high.
Temporary stairs on construction sites must be kept clear of stored materials, debris, and tripping hazards at all times.
Do not use a stairway that is still under construction unless it has been properly secured with handrails and is structurally complete.
discussion_prompt: What's the most common stairway hazard you see on a jobsite — and how can we fix it today?

title: Personal Fall Arrest Systems (PFAS)
talking_points: A PFAS consists of three components: a full-body harness, a connector (lanyard or retractable), and an anchorage point rated for at least 5,000 pounds per worker.
Maximum freefall distance is 6 feet. Maximum deceleration distance is 3.5 feet. Together with harness stretch, you need at least 18.5 feet of clearance below your anchorage.
The maximum arresting force on the body must not exceed 1,800 pounds — this is why shock-absorbing lanyards and retractables are used instead of plain rope.
After a fall arrest, the harness and all components must be removed from service, inspected by a competent person, and replaced if there is any sign of damage.
Prompt rescue must be planned before any PFAS use. A worker suspended in a harness can develop suspension trauma in as little as 15 minutes.
discussion_prompt: Do you know what your rescue plan is if someone on this crew takes a fall today — and how quickly can we get to them?

title: Guardrail Systems
talking_points: Top rails must be 42 inches high (plus or minus 3 inches) and able to withstand 200 pounds of force applied in any outward or downward direction.
Midrails are required and must be installed halfway between the top rail and the walking surface — approximately 21 inches high.
Toeboards at least 3.5 inches high are required where materials could fall from the platform onto workers below.
Wire rope guardrails are acceptable if flagged every 6 feet with visible material and tensioned to prevent more than 3 inches of deflection.
Never lean against a guardrail as a backrest or use it to support heavy loads — guardrails are designed to arrest a fall, not to bear working loads.
discussion_prompt: If you noticed a guardrail that was loose or wobbly, what would you do before continuing work in that area?

title: Safety Nets
talking_points: Safety nets must be installed as close under the work surface as practical, and never more than 30 feet below.
Nets must extend outward from the edge of the work surface: 8 feet for fall distances up to 5 feet, and up to 13 feet for falls of 10 feet or more.
Drop-test safety nets with a 400-pound sandbag before use and after any repair. The net must catch the bag without contacting any surface below.
Remove all accumulated debris from safety nets at least weekly or before debris could affect net performance.
Safety nets are most common in bridge work, high-rise steel erection, and long-duration elevated work where guardrails and PFAS are impractical.
discussion_prompt: What do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of safety nets compared to guardrails or harnesses?

title: Struck-By Hazards — Overview
talking_points: Struck-by is one of OSHA's Fatal Four — the four leading causes of construction fatalities. Objects that fly, fall, swing, or roll are the main threats.
Never position yourself under a suspended load — even momentarily. If a crane or hoist is moving material above you, move out from underneath.
Secure all tools and materials at height with tool lanyards, toeboards, debris nets, or enclosed tool bags to prevent them from falling on workers below.
Be aware of vehicles and mobile equipment — stay visible, make eye contact with operators, and stay outside the swing radius of excavators and cranes.
Hard hats, safety glasses, and high-visibility clothing are your last line of defense — wear them properly and inspect them daily.
discussion_prompt: Can you think of a time on this job where something fell or flew toward someone — what could have prevented it?

title: Hard Hat Requirements
talking_points: Type I hard hats protect from impacts to the top of the head. Type II hard hats protect from both top and lateral impacts — know which your site requires.
Electrical classes matter: Class E is rated for 20,000 volts, Class G for 2,200 volts, and Class C provides no electrical protection.
Inspect your hard hat daily — look for cracks, dents, fading, or a chalky texture in the shell, and check the suspension for tears or lost elasticity.
Replace the suspension system at least annually, or immediately if it shows damage. Replace the shell every 5 years or per the manufacturer's guidelines.
Do not drill holes in your hard hat, apply stickers over damage, wear it backward (unless designed for it), or store it in direct sunlight for extended periods.
discussion_prompt: How old is your hard hat's suspension — and when was the last time you replaced it?

title: Crane Operations — General
talking_points: Only a certified, qualified operator may operate a crane. Certification is type-specific and capacity-specific, and must be renewed every five years.
Before each shift, the operator must perform a visual inspection and functional test. A competent person must perform a more thorough monthly inspection.
Maintain at least 20 feet of clearance from power lines up to 350kV. For lines over 350kV, greater distances apply per the voltage table.
A designated signal person is required whenever the operator cannot see the load or the landing zone. Use standard hand signals per OSHA requirements.
Know the crane's load chart — never exceed the rated capacity for the current configuration, radius, and boom length.
discussion_prompt: What would you do if an operator asked you to guide a load near a power line?

title: Crane Signals and Communication
talking_points: A qualified signal person must be used when the operator cannot directly see the load or its intended landing zone.
Signal persons must meet OSHA qualification requirements — either by a third-party evaluation or by employer assessment documented in writing.
Standard hand signals are required unless voice communication (radio) is used. Both the operator and signal person must agree on the method before the lift.
Any person on site can give an emergency stop signal, and the operator must obey it regardless of who gave it.
Never give signals for fun or casually gesture near a crane — the operator may interpret it as a command and move the load.
discussion_prompt: Can you demonstrate the standard hand signal for 'stop' and 'emergency stop' — and what's the difference?

title: Rigging and Load Securement
talking_points: All slings — wire rope, synthetic, chain, or metal mesh — must have a minimum safety factor of 5:1 based on the rated capacity.
Inspect slings before each use. For wire rope, look for 10 or more broken wires in one rope lay, kinking, crushing, corrosion, or bird-caging.
Never wrap a sling around a sharp edge without padding. A sharp corner can cut through synthetic webbing in a single lift.
Know the sling angle — as the angle decreases from vertical, the load on each sling leg increases. At 30 degrees from horizontal, each leg carries twice the proportional load.
Shackles, hooks, and other hardware must match the sling rating. A 5-ton sling on a 3-ton shackle means your system is only rated for 3 tons.
discussion_prompt: What's the first thing you look for when inspecting a wire rope sling — and when was the last time you rejected one?

title: Overhead Loads and Barricading
talking_points: No worker should ever stand or walk under a suspended load. Barricade the area under and around any active lift zone.
Tag lines are required on loads that could swing, spin, or contact structures. The tag line operator must stay clear of the drop zone.
Barricade the full swing radius of the crane's boom and load. Workers outside the barricade should understand that the load can swing beyond its intended path.
Store materials away from edges where they could be knocked off by wind, vibration, or accidental contact — especially near multi-story openings.
If you see an unsecured load overhead, do not walk under it. Alert the crew and the operator immediately.
discussion_prompt: What's the best way to barricade a lift zone when there's a lot of foot traffic on site?

title: High-Visibility Clothing
talking_points: ANSI Class 2 high-visibility vests or shirts are the minimum for most construction work near vehicle traffic or mobile equipment.
Class 3 garments — which cover more of the body including the arms and legs — are required for work near high-speed traffic (over 50 mph) or in low-light conditions.
Retroreflective strips must be clean and intact. Faded, torn, or covered stripes reduce your visibility significantly — especially at dawn, dusk, and at night.
High-visibility clothing does not make you invincible. Always maintain situational awareness, make eye contact with equipment operators, and use designated walkways.
Replace high-vis garments when the background fluorescent fabric has faded or when retroreflective strips no longer reflect light when tested.
discussion_prompt: Take a look at your vest right now — are the reflective strips still bright, or is it time for a replacement?

title: Powered Industrial Trucks (Forklifts)
talking_points: Only trained and certified operators may operate a forklift. Certification must be renewed every three years, and re-evaluation is required after any incident.
Perform a pre-shift inspection every time — check brakes, steering, horn, lights, forks, mast, tires, and hydraulics before operating.
The load capacity plate must be visible and legible. Never exceed the rated capacity — remember that capacity decreases as the load center moves farther from the mast.
Pedestrians have the right of way, but don't count on it. Operators must slow down at intersections, sound the horn, and maintain clear sightlines.
Never allow riders on the forks, on the counterweight, or anywhere on the forklift not designed for passengers.
discussion_prompt: What's the most dangerous thing you've seen happen with a forklift — and how could it have been prevented?

title: Trenching and Excavation — Protective Systems
talking_points: A protective system — sloping, benching, shoring, or a trench shield — is mandatory for any trench 5 feet deep or more, unless the excavation is entirely in stable rock.
Soil classification determines the required slope: Type A (most stable) at 3/4:1, Type B at 1:1, and Type C (least stable) at 1.5:1. Most construction soil is Type B or C.
For trenches deeper than 20 feet, the protective system must be designed or approved by a Registered Professional Engineer.
Trench shields (trench boxes) protect workers from cave-ins but do not prevent the cave-in itself. They must extend at least 18 inches above the surrounding grade.
Never enter an unprotected trench — even a shallow one. Soil weighs about 100 pounds per cubic foot. A cubic yard of soil can weigh as much as a car.
discussion_prompt: If you arrived at a trench that had no protective system in place, what would you do — even if your foreman told you to get in?

title: Trenching and Excavation — Access and Egress
talking_points: A ladder, stairway, or ramp must be provided in trenches 4 feet deep or more. You must not travel more than 25 feet laterally to reach the exit.
Ladders must extend at least 3 feet above the top of the trench and be secured against displacement.
The spoil pile — the excavated dirt — must be placed at least 2 feet back from the edge of the trench to prevent material from falling in and adding surcharge load to the walls.
Heavy equipment, vehicles, and stored materials must also be kept back from the trench edge. Vibration from equipment can destabilize the soil.
In an emergency — water rushing in, the sound of cracking soil, or visible wall movement — exit immediately. Do not wait for instructions.
discussion_prompt: Can you see the nearest ladder from where you'd be standing in today's trench — or do we need to add one?

title: Trenching and Excavation — Competent Person
talking_points: A competent person must inspect the excavation, adjacent areas, and protective systems daily before work begins and after any rain, vibration, or other event that could change conditions.
The competent person must be able to identify existing and predictable hazards and have the authority to take immediate corrective action — including stopping work.
Soil classification is the competent person's responsibility. They must evaluate the soil type using at least one visual and one manual test (thumb penetration, ribbon, etc.).
If conditions change — unexpected water, utility crossings, or signs of soil movement — the competent person must reassess and may need to upgrade the protective system.
Every worker in and around the excavation should know who the competent person is for today's work. If you don't know, ask before entering.
discussion_prompt: Who is the competent person for today's excavation work — and when was the last inspection?

title: Machine Guarding — General
talking_points: Every point of operation, nip point, rotating shaft, and moving part that a worker could contact must be guarded.
The 7-foot rule: if rotating parts (fan blades, shafts, pulleys, belts) are less than 7 feet above the floor or working level, they must be enclosed or guarded.
Guard openings must be small enough to prevent fingers from reaching the hazard — for fan blade guards, the maximum opening is 0.5 inches.
Never remove or bypass a guard to speed up production. If a guard interferes with the task, report it so an engineering solution can be found.
Before performing any maintenance or adjustment on a guarded machine, lock out and tag out the energy source first.
discussion_prompt: Have you ever seen a machine running with a guard removed? What was the reason — and what's the safer alternative?

title: Machine Guarding — Abrasive Wheels
talking_points: Before mounting any abrasive wheel, perform a ring test — tap the wheel gently and listen for a clear ring. A dull thud indicates a crack; do not use the wheel.
The work rest must be adjusted to within 1/8 inch of the wheel face. A larger gap can pull material — or your fingers — into the wheel.
The tongue guard (the adjustable shield above the work rest) must be within 1/4 inch of the wheel surface.
Never exceed the RPM rating printed on the wheel. A wheel running above its rated speed can explode with extreme force.
Always wear a face shield over safety glasses when grinding. Safety glasses alone do not provide adequate protection from flying particles and wheel fragments.
discussion_prompt: When was the last time someone adjusted the work rest on our bench grinder — and is it within the 1/8 inch requirement right now?

title: Machine Guarding — Power Presses
talking_points: Power presses are responsible for a significant number of workplace amputations. Point-of-operation guards are mandatory and must prevent hands from entering the die area.
Anti-repeat mechanisms prevent the press from cycling more than once per actuation. These must be tested and verified weekly.
Two-hand trip controls require both hands to be on the buttons simultaneously, keeping them clear of the point of operation during the stroke.
Inspect clutch and brake mechanisms weekly. A press that does not stop reliably at the top of the stroke is immediately dangerous.
Pull-back devices must be properly adjusted to each operator. Retract straps that are too loose will not clear your hands in time.
discussion_prompt: What would you do if you noticed the press was occasionally double-stroking — even if it seemed minor?

title: Lockout/Tagout (LOTO)
talking_points: Before servicing or maintaining any machine, all hazardous energy sources — electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, chemical, thermal, and gravitational — must be isolated and controlled.
Each worker performing the service must apply their own personal lock and tag. Never rely on someone else's lock to protect you.
After locking out, attempt to restart the equipment to verify it is truly de-energized. This 'try' step is critical and often skipped.
Written energy control procedures are required for each machine or piece of equipment. A generic 'turn it off and lock it' procedure is not compliant.
LOTO procedures must be reviewed at least annually and updated whenever equipment is modified or new energy sources are introduced.
discussion_prompt: Can you walk through the lockout procedure for the piece of equipment you're working on today — from notification to verification?

title: Conveyor Safety
talking_points: Never reach into a moving conveyor to clear a jam, retrieve material, or make an adjustment. Shut it down and lock it out first.
Emergency stop devices must be accessible along the entire length of the conveyor. Know where every e-stop is located in your work area.
Nip points where the belt meets rollers, pulleys, or idlers must be guarded. These areas can pull in loose clothing, fingers, and hands in a fraction of a second.
No one should ride on a conveyor belt under any circumstances, even when it appears to be moving slowly.
Walkways along conveyors must be kept clear. Tripping near a moving conveyor dramatically increases the chance of contact with moving parts.
discussion_prompt: Where are the emergency stops on the conveyors in your work area — can you point to all of them right now?

title: Unprotected Moving Parts — Belts, Pulleys, Gears
talking_points: Vertical and inclined belts less than 7 feet above the floor must be fully enclosed — not just covered on one side.
Projecting shaft ends must not extend more than half the shaft diameter beyond the bearing, unless guarded. Even a smooth rotating shaft can grab clothing.
Gears, sprockets, and chain drives must be enclosed regardless of height if workers could come into contact with them during normal operations.
Loose clothing, jewelry, long hair, and lanyards are the most common items caught in rotating parts. Tie back hair, remove jewelry, and tuck in clothing before working near machinery.
If you hear an unusual noise — grinding, clicking, or vibration — from a belt or pulley system, shut the machine down and report it. That noise is often the warning before failure.
discussion_prompt: Are there any exposed belts, pulleys, or shafts in your work area that you think should be guarded?

title: Electrical Safety — General
talking_points: Electrocution is one of the Fatal Four causes of death in construction. It takes less than 100 milliamps — the amount of current through a 100-watt light bulb — to cause a fatal heart rhythm.
On construction sites, all 120-volt, single-phase, 15-, 20-, and 30-amp receptacle outlets on temporary power must be GFCI-protected, or covered by an AEGCP.
Before plugging in, inspect cords and tools for damage — frayed insulation, missing ground pins, cracked housings, or exposed wires. Remove damaged equipment from service.
Never use electrical equipment in wet conditions unless it is rated for wet use and protected by a GFCI.
Treat every wire and circuit as live until you have personally verified it is de-energized, locked out, and tested with a voltage detector.
discussion_prompt: Where is the nearest GFCI outlet or panel to where you're working today — and when was it last tested?

title: Lockout/Tagout — Electrical Systems
talking_points: Before any electrical work, the circuit must be de-energized at the source, locked with a personal lock, and tagged with your name and date.
After locking out, use a voltage tester to verify zero energy at the point of work. Test the tester on a known live source first to confirm it is functioning.
Stored energy — in capacitors, batteries, or UPS systems — must be discharged or isolated before work begins. Locking out the breaker alone may not be enough.
If multiple workers are involved, each person applies their own lock to the lockout device. The last person to finish removes the last lock.
Only the person who applied a lock may remove it. If that person is unavailable, your company's specific emergency lock-removal procedure must be followed — never cut someone else's lock.
discussion_prompt: What types of stored energy might still be present in a circuit after you've turned off the breaker?

title: Power Line Clearance
talking_points: Maintain at least 20 feet of clearance between any part of a crane (including the load line and load) and power lines up to 350kV.
For non-crane equipment — boom trucks, concrete pumps, excavators — maintain at least 10 feet from lines under 50kV.
Always assume overhead lines are energized unless the utility has confirmed de-energization in writing and installed visible grounds.
Designate a spotter whose sole job is to watch clearance when equipment operates near power lines. The spotter should do nothing else during the operation.
Electricity can arc through air — you do not have to physically touch a power line to be electrocuted. This is why minimum distances exist.
discussion_prompt: Are there any overhead power lines on or near this jobsite — and does everyone know the minimum clearance for the equipment we're using?

title: Extension Cords and Temporary Wiring
talking_points: Extension cords on construction sites must be hard-usage or extra-hard-usage rated (marked 'S,' 'ST,' 'SO,' 'STO,' or similar on the jacket).
The ground pin on every plug must be intact. A cord with a missing or bent ground pin must be removed from service immediately.
Do not splice or tape damaged cords — replace them. A taped splice is not a repair; it is a fire and shock hazard.
Extension cords are temporary — they are not a substitute for permanent wiring. Temporary wiring on construction sites should not exceed 90 days.
Protect cords from damage: route them overhead or use cord covers at ground level. Do not run them through doorways where they can be pinched or through standing water.
discussion_prompt: How many extension cords are you using today — and when was the last time you inspected each one?

title: Ground-Fault Protection (GFCIs)
talking_points: A GFCI detects an imbalance of as little as 5 milliamps between the hot and neutral conductors and trips the circuit in about 1/40th of a second — fast enough to prevent electrocution.
On construction sites, GFCIs are required on all temporary 120-volt, single-phase, 15-, 20-, and 30-amp receptacle outlets.
Test your GFCI before each use by pressing the 'test' button. The power should cut off immediately. Press 'reset' to restore power.
Portable (plug-in or cord-mounted) GFCIs are just as effective as panel-mounted breakers and are useful when working at outlets far from the panel.
GFCIs protect you from ground faults, but they do not protect against contact between hot and neutral conductors. They are one layer of protection, not the only one.
discussion_prompt: Have you ever had a GFCI trip while using a tool — what happened, and what did you check before resetting it?

title: Arc Flash and Electrical PPE
talking_points: An arc flash is an explosive release of energy caused by an electrical fault — temperatures can reach 35,000 degrees Fahrenheit, four times the surface of the sun.
NFPA 70E defines approach boundaries: limited, restricted, and prohibited. Only qualified workers may enter the restricted and prohibited boundaries.
Arc-rated clothing is categorized by PPE level (1 through 4) based on the incident energy at the working distance. Your site's arc flash analysis determines the required level.
Never wear synthetic fabrics (polyester, nylon) when working near energized equipment — they melt onto skin and worsen burn injuries. Use arc-rated cotton or treated fabrics.
Before working on or near energized equipment, review the arc flash label on the panel — it specifies the incident energy, working distance, and required PPE.
discussion_prompt: Do you know the arc flash PPE category for the electrical panels in your work area — and where that label is?

title: Overhead Power Line Awareness
talking_points: Overhead power line contact kills construction workers every year. Assume all lines are energized unless the utility confirms otherwise in writing.
For equipment operating near power lines under 50kV, the minimum clearance is 10 feet. For cranes, it is 20 feet regardless of voltage (up to 350kV).
Before bringing tall equipment — cranes, concrete pumps, excavators with raised booms — onto a site, survey the area for overhead lines and plan your approach.

If equipment contacts a power line: stay on the equipment, warn others to stay away, and call 911. If you must exit due to fire, jump clear without touching the equipment and the ground at the same time, then shuffle away.
Spotters, insulating links, and proximity alarms are additional layers of protection — but maintaining the required clearance distance is the primary defense.
discussion_prompt: Has anyone here ever worked near overhead power lines — what precautions were taken, and were they enough?

title: Respiratory Protection Program
talking_points: A written respiratory protection program is required whenever respirators are used — even voluntarily for dust comfort. The program must include selection, fit testing, training, and medical evaluation.
Fit testing is mandatory before first use and annually thereafter. Quantitative or qualitative methods may be used, but the test must match the respirator model and size you will wear.
A medical evaluation must be completed before fit testing. A physician or licensed health care professional determines if you can safely wear a respirator.
Facial hair that interferes with the seal — beards, stubble, long sideburns — is prohibited when using tight-fitting respirators. No exceptions.
Know the difference between air-purifying respirators (filter the air) and atmosphere-supplying respirators (provide clean air). IDLH environments require SCBA or supplied-air with escape capability.
discussion_prompt: When was your last fit test — and are you using the same make and model of respirator you were tested on?

title: Silica Exposure — Construction (Table 1)
talking_points: Respirable crystalline silica is found in concrete, brick, block, stone, morite, and sand. Cutting, drilling, grinding, or demolishing these materials releases silica dust.
The OSHA PEL for silica is 50 micrograms per cubic meter as an 8-hour time-weighted average. The action level is 25 µg/m³.
Construction employers can use Table 1 — a list of 18 common tasks with pre-defined engineering controls and respirator requirements. If you follow Table 1 fully, air monitoring is not required.
Common Table 1 controls include: wet cutting for saws, water sprays for jackhammers, and shrouds with HEPA vacuums for grinders.
Silicosis is irreversible lung scarring caused by silica exposure. It can develop after just a few years of unprotected exposure and there is no cure.
discussion_prompt: What silica-generating tasks are we doing today — and are we following the Table 1 controls for each one?

title: Silica Exposure — Common Tasks
talking_points: Concrete sawing (walk-behind or handheld): use a saw with integrated water delivery to the blade. If water is not feasible, use a HEPA vacuum shroud and an APF-10 respirator.
Jackhammering or chipping concrete: use a water spray to keep the point of impact wet. When outdoors, this may be sufficient — indoors, add respiratory protection.
Grinding or tuckpointing: use a grinder equipped with a dust shroud connected to a HEPA vacuum. This is one of the highest silica exposures in construction.
Sweeping dry concrete or masonry dust with a broom creates significant airborne silica. Use a HEPA vacuum or wet sweeping methods instead.
Housekeeping matters — silica dust that settles can become airborne again from foot traffic, wind, or equipment movement. Clean up as you go.
discussion_prompt: Are all of our saws and grinders equipped with the right dust controls today — and is the water supply connected?

title: Lead Exposure
talking_points: Lead exposure in construction most commonly occurs during demolition, paint removal, cutting or welding on painted steel, and bridge rehabilitation.
The OSHA PEL for lead is 50 micrograms per cubic meter (8-hour TWA). The action level is 30 µg/m³.
In construction, biological monitoring is required when airborne lead exceeds the action level. Medical removal is triggered at a blood lead level of 50 µg/dL.
Lead dust can be carried home on clothing and shoes, exposing your family. Use disposable coveralls, shower before leaving the site, and never take contaminated clothing home.
Eating, drinking, smoking, or applying cosmetics in lead-contaminated areas is prohibited. Wash your hands and face before any of these activities.
discussion_prompt: Does anyone know if the structure we're working on has lead-based paint — and how would we find out?

title: Asbestos Awareness
talking_points: Asbestos is present in many buildings constructed before 1980 — in floor tiles, insulation, roofing, siding, pipe wrapping, ceiling tiles, and joint compound.
The OSHA PEL for asbestos is 0.1 fibers per cubic centimeter as an 8-hour TWA. There is no safe level of exposure.
In construction, asbestos work is classified from Class I (highest risk — removal of thermal system insulation) to Class IV (custodial activities near asbestos materials).
If you suspect you have disturbed asbestos-containing material — it may look like white or gray fibrous insulation — stop work immediately, isolate the area, and notify your supervisor.
Only trained and licensed workers may perform asbestos abatement. Awareness training is required for anyone who may encounter asbestos during their work.
discussion_prompt: Has a pre-demolition asbestos survey been done for this project — and do you know where the asbestos-containing materials are?

title: Hazard Communication (HazCom / GHS)
talking_points: Every hazardous chemical on site must have a Safety Data Sheet (SDS) that is readily accessible to every worker — physically or electronically, in a language they understand.
GHS labels include six key elements: product identifier, signal word (Danger or Warning), hazard statements, precautionary statements, supplier info, and pictograms.

Know the nine GHS pictograms — skull and crossbones (toxic), flame (flammable), exclamation mark (irritant), corrosion, exploding bomb, health hazard (carcinogen), gas cylinder, environment, and oxidizer.
Your employer must maintain a written HazCom program that includes a chemical inventory, SDS management, labeling procedures, and employee training.
GHS Revision 7 is coming — chemical manufacturers must update SDS and labels by May 2026, and employers must update workplace programs by November 2026.
discussion_prompt: Can you find the SDS for the chemicals you're using today — and do you know how to read Section 2 (Hazard Identification)?

title: Welding Fume Exposure
talking_points: Welding fumes contain a mixture of metals and gases that can cause serious lung disease, neurological damage (from manganese), and cancer (from hexavalent chromium).
Ventilation — local exhaust or general mechanical — is required whenever welding is performed in enclosed or confined areas.
Welding on stainless steel, galvanized steel, or painted surfaces produces especially hazardous fumes. Respiratory protection is often required in addition to ventilation.
The PEL for hexavalent chromium is 5 µg/m³ — extremely low. Even short-duration stainless steel welding can exceed this limit without proper controls.
Position yourself upwind or to the side of the weld plume whenever possible. Your welding helmet does not protect you from fume inhalation.
discussion_prompt: What material are we welding today, and do we have adequate ventilation — or do we need respiratory protection?

title: Hydrogen Sulfide (H₂S) Awareness
talking_points: Hydrogen sulfide is a colorless gas that smells like rotten eggs at low concentrations — but at dangerous levels it deadens your sense of smell, so you cannot rely on odor as a warning.
OSHA limits are: 20 ppm ceiling, with a 50 ppm peak allowed for no more than 10 minutes. The IDLH level is 100 ppm.
H₂S is encountered in sewers, manholes, excavations near swamps or landfills, oil and gas operations, and wastewater treatment facilities.
H₂S is heavier than air and accumulates in low-lying areas — trenches, pits, and confined spaces. Always monitor before entering these areas.
At high concentrations, H₂S causes immediate unconsciousness and can be fatal within minutes. Rescue attempts without SCBA have killed more people than the original exposure.
discussion_prompt: Are we working near any sources of H₂S today — and do we have functioning gas monitors on site?

title: Carbon Monoxide Awareness
talking_points: Carbon monoxide (CO) is colorless, odorless, and tasteless — you cannot detect it without a monitor. The OSHA PEL is 50 ppm as an 8-hour TWA.
The primary source on construction sites is gas-powered equipment — generators, concrete saws, compressors, and heaters — operated in enclosed or poorly ventilated spaces.
Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, and fatigue. These are easily mistaken for heat exhaustion or the flu.
Never operate gasoline or propane-powered equipment inside a building without adequate ventilation. Position exhaust to blow away from occupied areas and air intakes.
If a CO monitor alarms, evacuate the area immediately, get to fresh air, and report the reading. Do not re-enter until the source is identified and the area is ventilated.
discussion_prompt: Do we have any gas-powered equipment running inside or near the building today — and where is the exhaust going?

title: Heat Illness Prevention
talking_points: Heat illness kills more construction workers than any other weather-related hazard. The three stages — heat cramps, heat exhaustion, heat stroke — can progress rapidly.
Water, rest, and shade are the foundation. Drink water every 15 to 20 minutes — do not wait until you are thirsty. Cold water is better than room-temperature water.
New workers and those returning from a week or more away must be acclimatized gradually — start with 20% of the normal workload on day one and increase by 20% each day.
Know the signs of heat stroke: confusion, slurred speech, loss of consciousness, hot dry skin, or seizures. This is a medical emergency — call 911 and cool the worker immediately.
OSHA's proposed rule would set a mandatory action trigger at a heat index of 80°F. Even before it takes effect, use that as your guideline.
discussion_prompt: What's the heat index expected to be today — and where is our nearest shade and water station?

title: Cold Stress — Frostbite and Hypothermia
talking_points: Cold stress occurs when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it. Wind chill, wet clothing, and direct contact with cold surfaces accelerate heat loss.
Hypothermia begins when core body temperature drops below 95°F. Symptoms include uncontrollable shivering, confusion, slurred speech, and drowsiness.
Frostbite affects exposed skin — fingers, toes, ears, nose — and can cause permanent tissue damage. Skin turns white or grayish-yellow and feels waxy or numb.
Dress in layers: a moisture-wicking base layer, an insulating middle layer, and a wind/waterproof outer layer. Change out of wet clothing immediately.
Schedule warm-up breaks in a heated shelter and use the buddy system — cold workers may not recognize their own symptoms.
discussion_prompt: What's the wind chill today, and do we have a heated break area nearby?

title: Confined Space Entry — Construction
talking_points: A confined space is any area large enough for a worker to enter, with limited means of entry or exit, and not designed for continuous occupancy — manholes, vaults, tanks, pits, and silos are common examples.
In construction, the host employer must share known hazard information with the controlling contractor, who coordinates between all entry employers on site.

Before entry, a competent person must evaluate the space and determine if it is permit-required — meaning it has or could develop a hazardous atmosphere, engulfment risk, converging walls, or other serious hazards.
An attendant must be stationed outside the space at all times during entry. The attendant monitors conditions and can order evacuation but must never enter the space to attempt rescue.
Continuous atmospheric monitoring is required during the entire entry — not just before. Conditions inside a confined space can change rapidly.
discussion_prompt: Who is our attendant today, and what is the procedure if conditions change while someone is inside the space?

title: Confined Space Entry — General Industry
talking_points: A permit-required confined space has one or more of these characteristics: hazardous atmosphere, engulfment potential, converging walls or floors, or any other recognized serious hazard.
An entry permit must be completed before anyone enters and must include: the space, date, authorized entrants, attendants, entry supervisor, hazards, controls, and rescue provisions.
The entry supervisor is responsible for verifying that all permit conditions are met, that monitoring equipment is calibrated, and that rescue services are available.
Atmospheric testing must follow a specific order: oxygen first (19.5–23.5%), then combustible gases (below 10% LEL), then toxic gases (specific to the space).
If conditions change or any permit condition is violated, all entrants must exit immediately and the permit is canceled.
discussion_prompt: Walk me through the entry permit for today's confined space — is every field filled out, and has the entry supervisor signed off?

title: Atmospheric Monitoring for Confined Spaces
talking_points: Test the atmosphere before entry in this order: oxygen (19.5–23.5% is safe), then LEL (below 10% for entry), then specific toxics (H₂S, CO, etc.).
Monitor continuously during the entire entry, not just at the start. Conditions inside a space can change due to work activities, chemical reactions, or weather.
Calibrate your gas monitor daily per the manufacturer's instructions. Bump-test it with known calibration gas before each use.
Test at multiple levels — top, middle, and bottom of the space — because gases stratify by weight. Methane rises; H₂S sinks.
If any reading exceeds the action threshold, evacuate the space immediately, ventilate, and retest before re-entry.
discussion_prompt: When was our gas monitor last calibrated, and who is responsible for monitoring the atmosphere during today's entry?

title: Confined Space Rescue Planning
talking_points: A rescue plan must be in place before any confined space entry begins. Rescue is not optional, and 'we'll figure it out' is not a plan.
Non-entry rescue — using a retrieval line and mechanical device to pull the entrant out from outside — is the preferred method whenever the space geometry allows it.
If entry rescue is required, the rescue team must practice making permit space rescues at least once every 12 months. The fire department may or may not meet this requirement — verify.
NFPA guidance recommends rescue capability within 4 minutes of notification. If your rescue service cannot meet this, you need a closer or on-site team.

More people have died trying to rescue workers from confined spaces than from the original incidents. Never enter a space to rescue someone without proper training, equipment, and atmosphere monitoring.
discussion_prompt: If someone collapsed inside a confined space right now, what is our rescue plan — and can we execute it in under 4 minutes?

title: Fire Prevention on Construction Sites
talking_points: At least one fire extinguisher rated 2A or higher is required for every 3,000 square feet of building area on a construction site.
The travel distance to a Class A extinguisher must not exceed 100 feet. For Class B (flammable liquid) hazards, the distance is 50 feet.
All extinguishers must be visually inspected monthly and receive annual maintenance. Record the date and inspector's initials on the tag.
In construction, a 55-gallon water drum with two pails or a 1/2-inch garden-type hose discharging 5 gallons per minute may substitute for a 2A-rated extinguisher.
Keep access routes to extinguishers clear at all times. In an emergency, seconds matter — a blocked extinguisher is useless.
discussion_prompt: Can you point to the nearest fire extinguisher from where you're standing right now — and is it the right type for this area?

title: Fire Extinguisher Use and Inspection
talking_points: Remember PASS: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, and Sweep side to side.
In general industry, the maximum travel distance to a Class A extinguisher is 75 feet — shorter than the 100-foot construction allowance.
Monthly visual inspections check: pressure gauge in the green zone, pin and tamper seal intact, no visible damage or corrosion, and clear access.
Annual maintenance must be performed by a qualified professional per NFPA 10. Internal examination is required every 6 years.
Only fight a fire if it is small (incipient stage), you have a clear escape route, the extinguisher is the correct type, and you have been trained. Otherwise, evacuate and call 911.
discussion_prompt: Has everyone on this crew been trained on how to use a fire extinguisher — and do you feel confident doing it?

title: Hot Work Permits
talking_points: A hot work permit is required before any welding, cutting, brazing, soldering, or grinding that produces sparks or open flame outside a designated hot work area.
Clear all combustible materials within a 35-foot radius of the hot work. If they cannot be moved, cover them with fire-resistant blankets or shields.
A fire watch must remain in the area during hot work and for at least 30 minutes after work is completed. The fire watch must have a charged extinguisher and know how to use it.
The hot work permit must be signed by an authorized person and posted at the work location. It is valid only for the shift and area specified.
Check the other side of walls, floors, and ceilings where you are performing hot work — sparks and heat can travel through openings, gaps, and conductive materials.
discussion_prompt: Do we have a hot work permit for today's welding or cutting — and who is assigned as fire watch?

title: Flammable and Combustible Liquids
talking_points: A flammable liquid has a flash point below 100°F — this includes gasoline, acetone, and many solvents. A combustible liquid has a flash point at or above 100°F — like diesel fuel.
No more than 25 gallons of flammable liquids may be stored outside of an approved storage cabinet or room. Use approved safety cans with spring-loaded caps.
Bonding and grounding are required when dispensing flammable liquids from one container to another to prevent static discharge and ignition.
Store flammable liquids away from ignition sources, exits, and stairways. Maintain at least 20 feet between storage and buildings (or as specified by code).
Vapor is the hazard — flammable vapors are heavier than air and travel along the ground to ignition sources. Ventilate the area and eliminate all ignition sources within range.
discussion_prompt: Where are our flammable liquids stored right now — and are they in approved containers with proper separation from ignition sources?

title: Compressed Gas Cylinder Safety
talking_points: Store and transport cylinders upright, secured with chains or straps to prevent them from falling. A falling cylinder can become a projectile if the valve breaks.
Valve caps must be in place whenever a cylinder is not in active use, being moved, or in storage. The cap protects the valve from damage.
Separate oxygen from fuel gases (acetylene, propane) by at least 20 feet or by a 5-foot-high noncombustible barrier with a 30-minute fire rating.
Never use oil, grease, or petroleum products on oxygen regulators, fittings, or valves. Oxygen under pressure reacts violently with hydrocarbons.
Never use a cylinder as a roller, support, or anything other than its intended purpose. Do not strike cylinders or use them near electrical arcs.
discussion_prompt: Are our gas cylinders stored properly right now — upright, secured, caps on, and with proper separation between oxygen and fuel gas?

title: LPG (Propane) Safety
talking_points: Store propane cylinders at least 20 feet from combustible materials and any building opening (doors, windows, air intakes).
Check for leaks using soapy water on all connections. Never use an open flame to check for gas leaks.
Cylinders must not be filled beyond 80% capacity — liquid propane expands with temperature increases, and overfilling can cause a catastrophic release.
When using propane heaters in enclosed spaces, ensure adequate ventilation for both combustion air and CO exhaust. Follow manufacturer spacing requirements.
If you smell propane (it has an added odorant that smells like rotten eggs or skunk), shut off the source, ventilate the area, eliminate ignition sources, and evacuate.
discussion_prompt: Are we using any propane on site today — and is the storage and ventilation set up correctly?

title: Manual Lifting and Back Safety
talking_points: OSHA does not set a specific weight limit, but the NIOSH lifting equation recommends a maximum of 51 pounds under ideal conditions — and conditions on a jobsite are rarely ideal.
Use proper technique: keep the load close to your body, bend at the knees (not the waist), keep your back straight, and avoid twisting while lifting.
When a load is too heavy or awkward for one person, use a team lift or mechanical aid — dolly, hand truck, hoist, or crane. Asking for help is not weakness.
Plan your lift before you pick anything up: know the weight, check your path for obstacles, and identify where you will set it down.
Repetitive lifting is cumulative — a 30-pound object lifted 100 times is as hard on your back as a few heavy lifts. Rotate tasks and take breaks.
discussion_prompt: What's the heaviest thing you've lifted this week — and could a mechanical aid or team lift have made it safer?

title: Material Storage and Housekeeping
talking_points: Stack materials on level, solid surfaces. Limit stack heights per material type: lumber no more than 20 feet, bricks no more than 7 feet.
Secure round stock (pipe, rebar, conduit) with blocking or chocks to prevent rolling. One loose piece at the bottom can bring down an entire stack.
Keep aisles and access routes clear at all times — both for daily work and for emergency egress. A cluttered path is a tripping hazard and a rescue obstacle.
Separate incompatible materials: keep oxidizers away from flammables, acids away from bases, and chemicals away from food and water supplies.
Good housekeeping prevents accidents. Clean up as you go — don't wait for the end of the shift. Nails, scraps, and debris cause trips and punctures.
discussion_prompt: Walk through your work area mentally — is there anything stacked or stored right now that could fall, roll, or block an exit?

title: Rigging Inspection and Sling Safety
talking_points: Inspect all slings before each use. For wire rope slings, look for 10 or more broken wires in one rope lay, kinking, crushing, corrosion, heat damage, or bird-caging.
Synthetic web slings: look for cuts, burns, melting, acid or alkali damage, and worn or broken stitching. Remove from service if any are found.
Chain slings: check for stretch (links elongated by more than 5%), gouges, nicks, corrosion, cracks, or bent links.
Always use softeners or corner protectors on sharp edges. A single lift over an unprotected edge can destroy a synthetic sling.
The rated capacity on the tag is for a vertical hitch. As the sling angle decreases, the capacity decreases — at 60 degrees from horizontal, capacity is reduced to 87%; at 45 degrees, to 71%.
discussion_prompt: Pick up the nearest sling and inspect it right now — does it pass inspection, or should it be taken out of service?

title: PPE — Hazard Assessment and Selection
talking_points: Your employer must conduct a written hazard assessment for each work area and task to determine what PPE is required. This is not optional.
As of January 2025, all PPE in construction must properly fit each worker — the days of one-size-fits-all are over. Harnesses, gloves, eye protection, and more must be individually sized.
PPE is the last line of defense, not the first. Engineering and administrative controls should reduce the hazard before PPE is relied upon.
Your employer must pay for most required PPE. Exceptions include prescription safety glasses, everyday steel-toed boots (if allowed for personal use), and weather gear.
Inspect your PPE before every use. Damaged PPE provides a false sense of security — it may fail exactly when you need it most.
discussion_prompt: Does all of your PPE fit properly right now — or is anything too loose, too tight, or uncomfortable enough that you avoid wearing it?

title: Eye and Face Protection
talking_points: All safety eyewear must be ANSI Z87.1 rated — look for the 'Z87' marking on the lens or frame. Non-rated sunglasses are not safety glasses.
Match the protection to the hazard: safety glasses with side shields for impact, goggles for chemical splash, face shields over glasses for grinding.
For welding, use the correct shade number: Shade 10-14 for arc welding (depending on amperage), Shade 3-6 for cutting and brazing.
Safety glasses must fit snugly. Gaps at the top, bottom, or sides allow debris to enter. If your glasses slide down your nose, get a better-fitting pair.
If you get something in your eye, use the nearest eyewash station. Do not rub your eye. Flush for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention.
discussion_prompt: Check your safety glasses right now — are they Z87 rated, and do they fit without gaps?

title: Hand Protection — Glove Selection
talking_points: Match the glove to the hazard: cut-resistant gloves for sharp materials, chemical-resistant gloves for solvents and acids, insulated gloves for heat, and leather for general construction.
Cut-resistant gloves are rated A1 through A9 under ANSI/ISEA 105 — know the cut level required for your task. Sheet metal and glass typically require A4 or higher.
Chemical gloves must match the specific chemical — no single glove material resists everything. Check the SDS for glove recommendations.
Do NOT wear gloves near rotating machinery, drill presses, or lathes. A glove can be caught and pull your hand into the machine faster than you can react.
Inspect gloves before use: look for tears, holes, thinning, and degradation. Replace them when they no longer provide the intended protection.
discussion_prompt: Are you wearing the right type of glove for the work you're doing today — and what hazard is it protecting you from?

title: Hearing Protection
talking_points: Hearing protection is required in construction when noise exceeds 90 dBA as an 8-hour TWA. In general industry, a hearing conservation program begins at the 85 dBA action level.
Hearing loss from noise is permanent and irreversible. By the time you notice it, significant damage has already occurred.
The Noise Reduction Rating (NRR) on the package is tested in a lab. In practice, subtract 7 from the NRR and divide by 2 to estimate real-world protection.
Foam earplugs must be rolled tightly, inserted deep into the ear canal, and held until they expand. Poorly inserted plugs can reduce protection by 50% or more.
If you have to shout to be heard by someone 3 feet away, the noise level is likely above 85 dBA and you should be wearing hearing protection.
discussion_prompt: Can you hear normal conversation right now without raising your voice — or are we in an area where hearing protection should be worn?

title: Foot Protection
talking_points: Safety footwear must meet ASTM F2413 standards. Look for the I/75 (impact) and C/75 (compression) ratings stamped inside the boot.
For work near electrical hazards, wear EH-rated boots that provide insulation against accidental contact with energized circuits up to 600 volts.
Metatarsal guards provide additional protection for the top of the foot and are recommended for heavy material handling, steel erection, and demolition.
Slip-resistant soles are essential for wet, oily, or smooth surfaces. Check the outsole condition regularly — worn treads offer little traction.
Replace safety boots when the sole separates, the toe cap is exposed, or the leather is torn or cracked. Worn-out boots are not safety boots.
discussion_prompt: Look at the soles of your boots — do they still have good tread, and are they the right type for the surfaces you're working on today?

title: High-Visibility and Reflective Clothing
talking_points: ANSI 107 defines three classes of high-visibility garments. Class 2 is standard for most construction sites. Class 3 is required for roadway work or low-light conditions.
High-vis garments work through two mechanisms: fluorescent fabric for daytime visibility and retroreflective strips for nighttime visibility. Both must be maintained.
Faded fluorescent fabric loses its effectiveness. If your vest has turned from bright yellow-green to a pale or washed-out color, it needs to be replaced.
Retroreflective strips must be clean and intact. Dirt, paint, or damage reduces reflectivity significantly — test by shining a flashlight on the strips.
High-visibility clothing must be worn as the outermost layer. Wearing a jacket over your vest defeats the purpose.
discussion_prompt: Is everyone on the crew wearing the correct class of high-vis for today's work conditions?

title: Fall Protection PPE — Harness Inspection
talking_points: Inspect your harness before every use: check all webbing for cuts, burns, fraying, chemical damage, UV degradation, and broken stitching.
Check all buckles, D-rings, and grommets for cracks, distortion, sharp edges, and corrosion. If hardware is bent or cracked, remove the harness from service.
The dorsal D-ring (center of the back, between the shoulder blades) is the primary fall arrest attachment point. Other D-rings are for positioning or retrieval only.
A harness must properly fit each worker per the 2025 PPE fit rule. A too-loose harness can shift during a fall and cause injury; too-tight restricts movement and blood flow.
Any harness that has arrested a fall must be immediately removed from service and inspected by a competent person. Most manufacturers recommend replacement after any fall arrest.
discussion_prompt: Put your harness on right now and have a partner check the fit — is it snug without restricting your movement?

title: Concrete and Masonry — Formwork
talking_points: Formwork and shoring must be designed by a qualified person to support all anticipated loads — wet concrete, workers, equipment, and impact loads.
Do not place concrete into forms until the shoring system has been inspected and verified by a competent person.
Formwork must not be stripped until the concrete has reached sufficient strength to support its own weight and any construction loads. Follow the engineer's stripping schedule.
Workers must not stand on or work under formwork that is being erected, stripped, or could collapse. Barricade the area below active form operations.
During cold weather, concrete curing is slower — do not assume the standard stripping schedule applies. Consult with the engineer if temperatures drop below 40°F.
discussion_prompt: Has the shoring been inspected today, and do we have the engineer's stripping schedule posted?

title: Concrete and Masonry — Post-Tensioning
talking_points: Post-tensioning involves stressing steel strands or tendons to extremely high forces. A strand that breaks or releases can travel hundreds of feet at lethal velocity.
No workers may stand behind stressing jacks during tensioning operations. The area behind the jack must be barricaded and cleared.
Follow the engineer's stressing sequence exactly. Out-of-sequence tensioning can cause uneven forces that lead to structural failure or strand blowout.
Inspect anchorage hardware before tensioning — damaged wedges, cracked bearing plates, or misaligned strands can cause failures under load.
After tensioning is complete and strands are cut, the remaining tail must be protected to prevent contact injuries from sharp wire ends.
discussion_prompt: Is the barricade set up behind all stressing jacks, and does everyone know to stay out of the strand path?

title: Demolition Safety
talking_points: An engineering survey must be completed before demolition begins, documenting the structure's condition, construction type, and any hazardous materials present.
Brace or shore adjacent structures and walls that may be affected by the demolition. Unplanned collapse of an adjacent wall is one of the leading causes of demolition fatalities.
Demolish structures systematically — work from top to bottom, outside to inside. Never undercut a load-bearing element.
Debris chutes are required when dropping material more than 20 feet. The area around the discharge end must be barricaded and a warning sign posted.
Utilities must be disconnected and verified dead before demolition. This includes electricity, gas, water, sewer, steam, and telecommunications.
discussion_prompt: Have all utilities been confirmed disconnected for today's demolition area — and who verified it?

title: Assured Equipment Grounding Conductor Program (AEGCP)
talking_points: An AEGCP is an alternative to GFCIs for protecting workers from ground faults on construction sites. Your site must use one or the other — not neither.
Under an AEGCP, all cord sets and receptacles must be visually inspected daily for damage, and defective equipment must be removed from service immediately.
Continuity and grounding conductor tests must be performed before first use on site and at least every three months thereafter.
A written program must be in place, and a competent person must be designated to implement and maintain the testing schedule.
Test records must be kept and made available to OSHA upon request. If you cannot show documentation of testing, the AEGCP is not compliant.
discussion_prompt: Is this site using GFCIs, an AEGCP, or both — and when was the last time grounding tests were performed?

title: Working on or Near Energized Equipment
talking_points: The default position is to de-energize before working. Live work is only permitted when de-energizing would create a greater hazard or is infeasible.
Only qualified electrical workers may work on or near exposed energized parts. A qualified worker must understand the specific hazards and safe work practices for the voltage involved.
NFPA 70E defines approach boundaries: limited, restricted, and prohibited. The distance depends on the voltage. Cross the restricted boundary only with proper PPE and an energized work permit.
An energized electrical work permit must be completed and approved before any justified live work. The permit documents the hazard analysis, PPE required, and safe work procedures.
Insulated tools rated for the voltage must be used when working near energized parts. Standard tools can become conductors.
discussion_prompt: Is there any energized work planned today — and if so, has an energized work permit been completed?

title: Hand and Power Tool Safety
talking_points: Use the right tool for the job. Improvising — using a wrench as a hammer or a screwdriver as a pry bar — damages the tool and creates hazards.
All power tools must have guards in place. Do not remove, modify, or bypass the guard to gain access or speed.
Electric power tools must be grounded (three-prong plug) or double-insulated (marked with a square-within-a-square symbol). Never remove the ground pin.
Inspect tools before each use: check for cracked housings, frayed cords, dull blades, loose handles, and mushroomed heads on chisels and punches.
Disconnect power tools before changing blades, bits, or accessories. For pneumatic tools, disconnect the air supply first.
discussion_prompt: Is there a damaged or worn-out tool in your kit right now that should be replaced?

title: Powder-Actuated Tools
talking_points: Only trained operators may use powder-actuated tools. You must carry your operator's card when using the tool.
Test-fire into a test material at the beginning of each shift to verify the tool is functioning properly.
Never point a powder-actuated tool at anyone, loaded or unloaded. Treat it with the same respect as a firearm.
Do not use in explosive or flammable atmospheres. The charge can ignite flammable vapors.
A guard is required on the muzzle end to protect against flying fragments. Check that it is intact before each use.
discussion_prompt: Is the operator using this tool today trained and carrying their card — and have they test-fired the tool this shift?

title: Pneumatic Tools
talking_points: All pneumatic hose connections must be secured with safety clips, wire, or other positive locking devices to prevent accidental disconnection under pressure.
Whip checks (safety cables across hose couplings) are required to restrain hoses if a connection fails. An unrestrained pressurized hose is a serious struck-by hazard.
Air pressure for cleaning purposes must not exceed 30 psi — and even then, a chip guard and appropriate PPE (safety glasses minimum) are required.
Never carry a pneumatic nailer with your finger on the trigger. Use bump-fire mode only when approved by site policy and never for overhead or awkward-angle work.
Disconnect the air supply before performing any maintenance, clearing jams, or adjusting the tool.
discussion_prompt: Are all of our pneumatic hose connections secured with whip checks today?

title: Bench Grinders and Cut-Off Saws
talking_points: Perform a ring test on all abrasive wheels before mounting. A clear ring means the wheel is sound; a dull thud means it is cracked and must be discarded.
The work rest must be within 1/8 inch of the wheel. The tongue guard must be within 1/4 inch. Adjust these before starting — not while the wheel is spinning.
Never exceed the RPM rating on the wheel. A wheel spinning above its rated speed can shatter with explosive force.
Wear a face shield over safety glasses when grinding. Safety glasses alone do not protect against a wheel burst or large flying particles.
Let the grinder reach full speed before applying material to the wheel. Do not force material into the wheel — let the abrasive do the work.
discussion_prompt: When was the last time the work rest and tongue guard on our bench grinder were adjusted — and are they within spec?

title: Chainsaws and Brush Clearing
talking_points: Required PPE for chainsaw operation includes chainsaw chaps or pants, a face screen or safety glasses, hearing protection, hard hat, and gloves.
Test the chain brake before each use — it must stop the chain immediately. The chain brake is your primary protection against kickback.
Drop-starting a chainsaw (holding it in the air and pulling the cord) is prohibited. Start it on the ground with the chain brake engaged.
Maintain a two-person awareness zone — know where others are working and maintain safe distances. A chain can throw debris 50 feet or more.
Watch for spring poles (bent trees under tension), dead limbs overhead (widowmakers), and lean direction before making any cut.
discussion_prompt: Is everyone wearing the correct PPE for today's cutting work — including chaps and face protection?

title: Backing and Spotters
talking_points: A spotter is required whenever the vehicle operator's view to the rear is obstructed. The spotter must be in the operator's line of sight at all times.
Establish clear hand signals or radio communication between the spotter and the operator before backing begins. Both must agree on the signals.
Backup alarms must be functional on all construction vehicles. Test them at the beginning of each shift.
Pedestrians must stay outside the backing zone. If you cannot see the operator's mirrors, the operator cannot see you.
Never walk behind a vehicle that is running or has its reverse lights on. Assume the vehicle will move.
discussion_prompt: Do we have spotters assigned for today's backing operations — and have signals been reviewed?

title: Dump Truck and Haul Road Safety
talking_points: Berms or guardrails at least mid-axle height are required along the edges of haul roads where a drop-off exists.
Check overhead clearance before raising the dump bed — contact with power lines, bridges, or structures is a leading cause of dump truck fatalities.
Walk around the truck before operating. Check tires, brakes, lights, mirrors, and the tailgate. Know the truck's blind spots.
No riders are permitted in the bed of a dump truck. Material can shift during transport and crush a person.
On grades, use the appropriate gear and maintain safe following distances. A loaded dump truck takes significantly longer to stop.
discussion_prompt: Are there any overhead hazards on our haul route today — power lines, low clearances, or overhanging structures?

title: Work Zone Traffic Control (Flagging)
talking_points: Only trained flaggers may direct traffic in work zones. Training must cover the MUTCD requirements for flagging operations.
Flaggers must wear Class 2 high-vis vests during the day and Class 3 at night, with retroreflective material visible from all directions.
Use a STOP/SLOW paddle — it is the standard traffic control device. Flags are only permitted for emergency situations.
Position yourself where you are visible to approaching traffic and have an escape route if a vehicle does not stop. Never turn your back on traffic.
Flagging is one of the most dangerous tasks in construction. Stay alert, stay sober, and do not use your phone while directing traffic.
discussion_prompt: Does our flagger today have an escape route identified — and can approaching drivers see them from a safe stopping distance?

title: Mobile Crane Setup and Inspection
talking_points: Set up the crane on level, firm ground. Outriggers must be fully extended and set on adequate blocking or cribbing — never on soft or undermined ground.
Review the load chart before every lift. The rated capacity depends on the configuration: boom length, radius, quadrant of operation, and whether outriggers are extended.
A pre-shift visual inspection by the operator is required. Monthly inspections by a competent person and annual inspections by a qualified person must also be documented.
Check the swing radius — the area the counterweight sweeps must be barricaded or otherwise protected to prevent workers from being struck or crushed.
Before the first lift, verify that all safety devices — LMI (load moment indicator), anti-two-block, boom angle indicator — are functional.
discussion_prompt: Has the load chart been reviewed for today's heaviest planned lift — and are the outriggers on adequate support?

title: Mast Climbing Work Platforms
talking_points: Mast climbing platforms must be erected, operated, and dismantled according to the manufacturer's instructions by trained workers.
Daily inspections must include mast connections, platform decking, guardrails, drive systems, and safety devices (overload sensors, wind speed limits).
Observe the manufacturer's wind speed limits — most platforms must be lowered when wind exceeds 25-30 mph, depending on the model.
The base must be on a firm, level foundation with adequate capacity. Tie-backs to the structure are required at the intervals specified by the manufacturer.
Workers on the platform must be trained in its operation and emergency procedures, including manual lowering in case of power failure.
discussion_prompt: What are the wind speed limits for the mast climber we're using — and what is the procedure if the wind picks up?

title: System Scaffolds (Frame Scaffolds)
talking_points: Frame scaffolds must be erected per the manufacturer's instructions with cross-bracing installed on both sides at every level.
Base plates and mudsills are required. The mudsill must distribute the load to prevent the scaffold from sinking into soft ground.
Scaffold must be plumb and level. If the base is out of level, the entire structure above is compromised — do not use shims or scraps to level frames.
A competent person must inspect frame scaffolds before each work shift and after any event that could affect structural integrity (wind, impact, rain).
Do not exceed the rated load capacity. This includes workers, tools, and materials on each platform level.
discussion_prompt: Is the scaffold we're using today plumb and level — and when was the last competent person inspection?

title: Housekeeping on Construction Sites
