talking_points: Good housekeeping prevents injuries. Trips, slips, and falls from poor housekeeping are among the most common construction injuries.
Remove or bend down protruding nails from boards and formwork as you go. A nail puncture through a boot can cause a serious infection.
Keep walkways, stairways, and access routes clear of debris, tools, cords, and stored materials at all times.
Use designated waste containers — separate construction debris from hazardous waste. Do not allow waste to accumulate in work areas.
Clean up at the end of every task, not just at the end of the shift. The worker who comes after you deserves a clean, safe work area.
discussion_prompt: Look around your work area right now — is there anything that could cause a trip, slip, or fall that we should address before we start?

title: Slips, Trips, and Falls — Walking Surfaces
talking_points: Walking surfaces must be kept dry, clean, and in good repair. Wet floors must be marked or barricaded until they are dry or mats are placed.
Cord management prevents trips — route cords overhead, through conduit, or use cord covers. Never run cords across walkways without protection.
Adequate lighting is essential. If you cannot see the walking surface clearly, you cannot identify hazards. Report burned-out lights immediately.
Wear footwear appropriate for the surface — slip-resistant soles for wet or oily areas, treaded boots for uneven terrain.
Report damaged flooring, raised thresholds, loose carpet, broken tiles, and uneven surfaces immediately. A quick repair prevents a serious injury.
discussion_prompt: What's the most common tripping hazard you encounter in your daily work — and how can we eliminate it?

title: Stacking and Storage — Material Yards
talking_points: Lumber must be stacked no higher than 20 feet and cross-piled to create stability. Remove nails from used lumber before stacking.
Brick stacks must not exceed 7 feet in height. Taper the stack back 2 inches for every foot above 4 feet.
Round stock — pipe, rebar, conduit — must be blocked or chocked to prevent rolling. One displaced chock can release an entire pile.
Never lean materials against walls or structures where they could slide or be knocked over. Secure them flat or in racks.
Leave sufficient aisle space between stacks for workers and equipment to pass safely — typically at least 3 feet, more for forklift access.
discussion_prompt: Is there any material in our storage area that could fall, roll, or collapse if bumped — and what should we do about it?

title: Noise Exposure and Hearing Conservation
talking_points: The OSHA PEL for noise is 90 dBA over an 8-hour TWA with a 5 dB exchange rate — meaning every 5 dB increase halves the allowable exposure time. At 100 dBA, you have 2 hours.
In general industry, the 85 dBA action level triggers a full hearing conservation program including monitoring, audiometric testing, and training. Construction has no equivalent requirement.
Impulse noise (nail guns, powder-actuated tools, explosions) must not exceed 140 dB peak sound pressure level.
Noise-induced hearing loss is cumulative and permanent. It happens gradually — most workers do not notice until significant damage has occurred.
Engineering controls (quieter equipment, barriers, isolation) are preferred over relying solely on hearing protection. But when PPE is needed, insert it properly every time.
discussion_prompt: What are the loudest tasks we perform regularly — and are we using hearing protection consistently for all of them?

title: Bloodborne Pathogens
talking_points: Bloodborne pathogens — including HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C — can be transmitted through contact with infected blood or other potentially infectious materials.
Practice universal precautions: treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious regardless of the source.
Your employer must have a written exposure control plan and must offer the Hepatitis B vaccine series to workers with occupational exposure — at no cost.
Use appropriate PPE — gloves at minimum — when providing first aid or cleaning up blood. Wash hands immediately after removing gloves.
Dispose of contaminated sharps in puncture-resistant, labeled containers. Never recap, bend, or break needles.
discussion_prompt: Where is the nearest first aid kit with gloves, and do you know the procedure if you're exposed to blood on the job?

title: Sanitation — Toilets, Water, Hygiene
talking_points: At least one toilet facility is required for every 20 workers on a construction site. Facilities must be maintained in a sanitary condition.
Potable drinking water must be provided and clearly labeled. Non-potable water (used for dust control, cleaning, etc.) must be labeled to prevent drinking.
Single-use drinking cups must be provided with the water supply. Shared cups or bottles spread illness.
Handwashing facilities must be available. At minimum, hand sanitizer may be used, but soap and water is preferred — especially before eating and after using the restroom.
On sites with hazardous material exposure (lead, silica, chemicals), workers must wash hands and face before eating, drinking, or smoking.
discussion_prompt: Are our portable toilets clean and adequately stocked — and do we have enough for the number of workers on site?

title: Crystalline Silica Medical Surveillance
talking_points: Medical surveillance is required for workers exposed above the action level (25 µg/m³) for 30 or more days per year.
The initial exam must occur within 30 days of assignment and includes a medical history, physical exam, chest X-ray, and pulmonary function test.
Follow-up exams are required every three years for workers who remain exposed above the action level.
The examining physician must be informed of the worker's exposure level, respirator use, and the specific tasks performed.
Workers must receive a copy of the physician's written medical opinion. If the doctor recommends limitations, the employer must accommodate them.
discussion_prompt: Are there workers on this crew who should be enrolled in silica medical surveillance — and is everyone current on their exams?

title: Pile Driving Safety
talking_points: A competent person must inspect the pile driving equipment — hammer, leads, helmet, and cap — daily before use.
No workers may be under the hammer or pile at any time during driving operations. Clear the area and establish exclusion zones.
Adequate blocking must be used to support piles during positioning to prevent them from falling before driving begins.
Hearing protection is mandatory — pile driving generates extreme noise levels well above the 90 dBA PEL.
Watch for bounceback and misalignment — a pile that shifts during driving can release suddenly and strike nearby workers.
discussion_prompt: Is the exclusion zone set up for today's pile driving — and is everyone wearing hearing protection?

title: Marine and Barge Operations
talking_points: Personal flotation devices (PFDs) are required for workers over or adjacent to water where the danger of drowning exists — generally within 25 feet of water's edge.
Ring buoys with at least 90 feet of line must be provided every 200 feet along the water's edge.
A rescue skiff must be immediately available at locations where workers are over water. 'Available' means crewed, fueled, and ready to deploy.
Barge decks are walking-working surfaces — keep them clear of tripping hazards, and ensure guardrails are in place on open edges.
Weather and water conditions can change quickly. Monitor forecasts and suspend operations during severe weather, high winds, or dangerous currents.
discussion_prompt: Is everyone near the water wearing a PFD right now — and where is the nearest ring buoy and rescue skiff?

title: Underground Construction (Tunneling)
talking_points: Check for hazardous gases before entry and continuously during work. Oxygen must be at least 19.5%, and H₂S action level in tunnels is 5 ppm.
An emergency escape plan must be established, communicated, and drilled. Every worker must know the primary and secondary escape routes.
Fire-resistant hydraulic fluid must be used in underground equipment. A hydraulic line burst with standard fluid in an enclosed space creates an immediate fire risk.
Ground support and ventilation systems must be inspected regularly by a competent person. Changing ground conditions require reassessment.
Communication systems must be maintained between the surface and the underground work area at all times.
discussion_prompt: Can everyone identify the emergency exits and communication points in our underground work area?

title: Steel Erection — General
talking_points: A site-specific erection plan must be prepared before steel erection begins, addressing the sequence of erection, crane procedures, and fall protection.
Anchor bolts: a minimum of four bolts per column must be installed in the concrete pier or footing before columns are set.
No loads may be placed on the steel structure until connections are secured and sufficient structural stability has been achieved.
Column splices must be designed to resist construction loads. Temporary guying, bracing, or shoring may be required until permanent connections are completed.
All workers involved in steel erection must receive training specific to the hazards of steel erection — this is in addition to general fall protection training.
discussion_prompt: Has the erection plan been reviewed with the crew today — and does everyone understand the sequence?

title: Concrete Pumping Operations
talking_points: Before positioning the pump boom, survey the area for overhead power lines. The boom must maintain required clearance distances at all times.
Pipeline restraints are required at bends and connections to prevent whipping if a coupling fails under pressure.
Clean-out is one of the most hazardous phases — compressed air used to purge the line can propel a sponge ball or concrete with lethal force. Clear the discharge area.
Operators must be trained on the specific pump model, including emergency shutdown procedures and boom operation limits.
Ensure the pump is set up on stable, level ground with outriggers fully deployed. Ground conditions must support the combined weight of the pump and the concrete load.
discussion_prompt: Are there any overhead lines near our pump setup today — and is the clean-out area barricaded?

title: Tower Crane Operations
talking_points: Tower crane foundations must be designed and certified by a Professional Engineer. The foundation must account for soil conditions, crane loads, and weather forces.
Climbing (jacking) operations must follow the manufacturer's procedures exactly. Only trained personnel may perform climbing operations.
In high winds, the crane must be taken out of service and the boom set to weather vane (free-slew) per the manufacturer's wind speed limits.
Anti-collision systems are required when multiple cranes overlap in their operating radii. Coordination between operators is critical.
Daily operator inspections and monthly competent person inspections must be documented. Report any unusual noises, vibrations, or warning indicators immediately.
discussion_prompt: What is the wind speed limit for our tower crane, and what is the procedure when it is exceeded?

title: Structural Steel — Bolting and Welding
talking_points: At least two bolts must be installed and tightened at each connection before the crane releases the load. This is the minimum for structural stability.
Fall protection is required for connectors above 15 feet and for all other ironworkers above 6 feet (or 30 feet for decking in a controlled decking zone).
Welded connections on structural steel must be performed by certified welders using approved procedures. Inspect joints visually and per the inspection plan.
Temporary bracing may be required until permanent connections are completed. Do not remove temporary bracing until the engineer authorizes it.
Bolt inspection (torque verification or turn-of-nut method) must be performed per the project specifications. Under-torqued bolts compromise structural integrity.
discussion_prompt: Are all connections in today's work area secured with at least two bolts — and has anyone verified the torque?

title: Oxy-Fuel Cutting and Welding
talking_points: Store oxygen cylinders at least 20 feet from fuel gas cylinders, or separate them with a 5-foot-high noncombustible barrier with a 30-minute fire rating.
Flashback arrestors must be installed on both the torch end and the regulator end of the hoses. Check valves alone are not sufficient.
Before lighting the torch, purge each hose individually to remove any mixed gases. Open fuel gas first when lighting; close fuel gas last when shutting down.
Never use oil, grease, or any petroleum-based product on oxygen equipment. Oxygen under pressure plus hydrocarbons equals an explosive reaction.
Inspect hoses for cracks, burns, and leaks before each use. Replace damaged hoses — do not tape them.
discussion_prompt: Are our cylinders separated properly right now — and do our torches have flashback arrestors on both ends?

title: Arc Welding Safety
talking_points: Electrode holders must be rated for the maximum amperage of the welder. Using an undersized holder creates a fire and shock hazard.
The work lead (ground clamp) should be attached as close to the weld area as practical. A long return path increases resistance and shock risk.
Welding cables must be inspected for damaged insulation before each use. Exposed conductors can deliver a fatal shock, especially in damp conditions.
Wear dry gloves and clothing. Even low-voltage welding circuits (60-80V open circuit) can kill, particularly in wet or confined conditions.
Provide adequate ventilation — welding fumes contain metals that can cause serious respiratory and neurological damage.
discussion_prompt: Is the welding area properly ventilated today — and has the work lead been placed close to the weld point?

title: Welding in Confined Spaces
talking_points: All cylinders and welding machines must remain outside the confined space. Only the torch and leads enter the space.
Mechanical ventilation is mandatory when welding in a confined space. Natural ventilation alone is never sufficient.
Continuous atmospheric monitoring for oxygen, LEL, and toxic gases must be performed throughout the welding operation.
A fire watch must be stationed both inside (if possible) and outside the space. Sparks and slag can accumulate in hidden areas.
When welding is interrupted for a substantial period — like a lunch break — remove the electrode from the holder and shut off the gas supply.
discussion_prompt: If we're welding inside a space today, are the cylinders outside, the ventilation running, and a fire watch in place?

title: Concrete Finishing — Knee and Back Safety
talking_points: Knee pads are essential for concrete finishers. Prolonged kneeling on hard surfaces causes bursitis, cartilage damage, and chronic knee pain.
Use kneeling boards to distribute your weight across a larger area. This reduces point-pressure on the knees and provides a more stable surface.
Rotate tasks throughout the day to avoid sustained kneeling or bending. Alternate between finishing, forming, and other activities when possible.
Long-handled finishing tools (bull floats, fresnos, power trowels) reduce the need to bend and kneel. Use them whenever the task allows.
Stretch before the shift and during breaks. Focus on hamstrings, lower back, and quadriceps — the muscle groups most stressed by finishing work.
discussion_prompt: Is everyone wearing knee pads today — and when was the last time we rotated tasks to give knees and backs a break?

title: Tilt-Up Construction
talking_points: Temporary bracing for tilt-up panels must be designed by a Professional Engineer and installed before the crane releases the panel.
At least two braces per panel are required. Braces must be secured to both the panel and the floor slab at the specified locations.
No one may work or walk on the side of a panel opposite the braces during erection — if the panel falls, it falls toward the unbraced side.
Rigging hardware — inserts, strongbacks, and lifting clutches — must be inspected before each lift and must match the panel weight.
Wind is the enemy of tilt-up erection. Monitor wind speed continuously and suspend operations when speeds exceed the engineer's limits for the panel size.
discussion_prompt: Are the braces installed per the engineer's plan, and is anyone working on the unbraced side of a panel right now?

title: Electrical Panels and Clearances
talking_points: A minimum of 36 inches of clear working space is required in front of electrical panels rated up to 600 volts. This space must be kept free of storage, materials, and equipment.
The working space must be at least 30 inches wide and extend from floor to 6.5 feet high (or to the height of the equipment, whichever is greater).
All panel directories must be labeled accurately. Every circuit breaker must be identified — blank or incorrect labels create hazards during lockout and emergencies.
Panels must be accessible — never locked in rooms where only one person has the key, and never placed behind barriers that prevent quick access.
Report any panels with missing covers, exposed wiring, or signs of overheating (discoloration, burning smell) immediately.
discussion_prompt: Are all the electrical panels in our work area accessible with 36 inches of clearance — and are the directories current?

title: First Aid and Emergency Response
talking_points: A first aid kit must be available on every construction site. Its contents must be appropriate for the hazards present and be checked regularly to replace used items.
At least one person trained in first aid and CPR must be available within 3-4 minutes of any work area where there is no infirmary, clinic, or hospital in near proximity.
Emergency phone numbers — 911, the site safety contact, and the nearest hospital — must be posted and known by all workers.
Know the location of the nearest AED (automated external defibrillator) if one is available. In cardiac arrest, defibrillation within 3-5 minutes dramatically improves survival.
Do not move an injured person unless they are in immediate danger. Spinal injuries can be worsened by improper movement. Wait for trained medical responders.
discussion_prompt: Where is the nearest first aid kit and AED, and who on this crew is trained in CPR?

title: Emergency Action Plans
talking_points: Every site must have a written emergency action plan covering fire, severe weather, medical emergencies, chemical spills, and structural collapse.
The alarm system — whether a horn, siren, or PA — must be understood by all workers. Know what different signals mean.
Evacuation routes must be posted, marked, and kept clear. Know your primary and alternate routes from your work area.
A headcount procedure must be in place. After evacuation, a designated person must verify that all workers are accounted for at the assembly point.
Drills should be conducted at least annually — more often on large or high-hazard sites. Drills reveal problems that a written plan cannot.
discussion_prompt: Where is our assembly point, and who is responsible for the headcount?

title: Severe Weather Preparedness
talking_points: Lightning: when thunder is heard less than 30 seconds after a lightning flash, stop outdoor work and seek shelter immediately. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
High wind thresholds vary by activity. Cranes typically have limits of 20-30 mph; mast climbers 25-30 mph. Know the limits for your equipment.
Tornado preparedness: identify the nearest interior room or structure on the lowest floor. Open construction sites may not have adequate shelter — plan your response in advance.
Heavy rain creates slip hazards, destabilizes excavations, and increases the risk of electrical faults. Reassess conditions before resuming work after a storm.
Designate a weather watcher — someone monitoring conditions and forecasts who has the authority to call for an evacuation.
discussion_prompt: What is the severe weather plan for today — and who is our weather watcher?

title: Spill Prevention and Cleanup
talking_points: A Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure (SPCC) plan is required for facilities storing more than 1,320 gallons of oil/petroleum products in aggregate.
Secondary containment — berms, dikes, or drip pans — must be in place around bulk storage to capture spills before they reach the ground or waterways.
Spill kits must be readily accessible near all chemical and fuel storage areas. Know the contents: absorbent pads, booms, gloves, bags, and instructions.
Report any spill above the reportable quantity to your supervisor immediately. Some spills require notification to state or federal agencies within a specific timeframe.
Only trained personnel should clean up chemical spills. If you don't know what was spilled, do not attempt cleanup — evacuate the area and notify your supervisor.
discussion_prompt: Where is the nearest spill kit, and does everyone know how to use it?

title: Stormwater and Erosion Control
talking_points: A Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) is required for construction sites that disturb more than 1 acre of land.
Best Management Practices include silt fencing, inlet protection, construction entrances with gravel tracking pads, and sediment basins.
Inspect erosion controls weekly and after every rain event that produces runoff. Repair or replace damaged controls within 24 hours.
Never discharge concrete washout, paint, solvents, or construction debris into storm drains, ditches, or waterways. Use designated washout areas.
Everyone on site shares responsibility for stormwater compliance. If you see a failed silt fence, an open storm drain, or a discharge, report it immediately.
discussion_prompt: After the last rain, did anyone inspect our silt fencing and inlet protection — and are they still functioning?

title: Asphalt Paving Safety
talking_points: Hot-mix asphalt is delivered at 275-325°F. Contact with skin causes immediate severe burns. Wear long sleeves, long pants, and boots at all times near hot mix.
Asphalt fumes can irritate the respiratory system. Work upwind when possible, and use respiratory protection if exposure is prolonged or in enclosed areas.
Release agents used to prevent asphalt from sticking must be approved — diesel fuel is not an acceptable release agent due to skin absorption and fire risk.
Traffic exposure is a leading cause of paving crew fatalities. Maintain work zone traffic control per the MUTCD and wear Class 2 or 3 high-visibility clothing.
Heat stress is compounded by the radiant heat from hot asphalt. Increase water intake and take more frequent breaks when paving in hot weather.
discussion_prompt: Are we upwind of the paver today, and is everyone wearing the right protective clothing for hot-mix work?

title: Roofing — Built-Up and Torch-Applied
talking_points: Torch-applied roofing requires a fire watch during application and for at least 2 hours after the last torch is extinguished.
A fire extinguisher must be within 6 feet of any active torch operation on a roof.
Hot asphalt kettles must be positioned at least 20 feet from any structure or combustible material. Monitor the kettle temperature continuously.
Check the roof deck before torching — gaps, cracks, and openings allow heat to reach combustible substrates below, which is a leading cause of roof fires.
Fall protection is required for all roofing work at 6 feet — the fire risk does not excuse fall protection. Combine fire safety and fall protection in your plan.
discussion_prompt: Who is the fire watch today, and do they have a charged extinguisher within reach?

title: Glazing and Curtain Wall Installation
talking_points: Fall protection is required at 6 feet during all glazing and curtain wall operations. PFAS is typically required because guardrails may interfere with the installation.
Secure glass panels with suction cups rated for the panel weight. Inspect suction cups for wear, cracking, and proper vacuum before each use.
Wind is the primary enemy of glass handling at height. Establish wind speed limits and suspend panel hoisting when limits are exceeded.
Panels staged at height must be secured against wind, vibration, and accidental displacement. An unsecured panel can become a sail in a gust.
Wear cut-resistant gloves when handling glass. Even tempered glass edges can cause deep cuts.
discussion_prompt: What are our wind speed limits for panel handling today — and who is monitoring conditions?

title: Elevator and Escalator Installation
talking_points: Elevator shaft openings at every floor must be guarded with guardrails to prevent falls into the shaft. This applies throughout construction.
The elevator car hoisting mechanism must be rated for the intended load and tested before use. Overloading the car is prohibited.
Never ride on top of an elevator car unless specifically authorized and equipped with fall protection tied to an independent anchorage.
Lockout/tagout is required before any work on elevator or escalator mechanisms. The power supply, hydraulic system, and counterweight must all be secured.
Communication between workers at the top and bottom of the shaft is essential. Use radios or an intercom system — do not shout.
discussion_prompt: Are all elevator shaft openings guarded on every floor right now — or are any guardrails missing?

title: Repetitive Motion and Ergonomic Awareness
talking_points: Repetitive motion injuries — carpal tunnel, tendinitis, rotator cuff strain — develop slowly over weeks and months but can become career-ending.
Take micro-breaks every 30-60 minutes during repetitive tasks. Even a 30-second pause to stretch and reset your posture makes a difference.
Maintain neutral wrist and shoulder positions whenever possible. Avoid sustained gripping, pinching, or reaching above shoulder height.
Vary your tasks throughout the day. If you've been drilling overhead for an hour, switch to a ground-level task before your muscles fatigue.
If you feel numbness, tingling, or persistent pain in your hands, wrists, arms, or shoulders, report it early. Early intervention prevents permanent damage.
discussion_prompt: Is anyone experiencing numbness, tingling, or pain from repetitive tasks — and can we rotate assignments today to help?

title: Vibration Exposure — Hand-Arm (HAVS)
talking_points: Hand-Arm Vibration Syndrome (HAVS) causes white fingers, numbness, tingling, and loss of grip strength. It is irreversible once advanced.
OSHA does not have a specific PEL for vibration, but NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to high-vibration tools (jackhammers, chipping guns, grinders) to less than 4 hours per day.
Anti-vibration gloves can reduce some transmission but are not a substitute for limiting exposure time. Choose gloves specifically rated for vibration reduction.
Maintain tools properly — dull bits, worn bearings, and imbalanced wheels increase vibration significantly. A well-maintained tool vibrates less.
If your fingers turn white or numb after using vibrating tools, report it to your supervisor and see a doctor. Early symptoms are the warning — don't ignore them.
discussion_prompt: How much time are you spending on vibrating tools each day — and are you rotating with other crew members?

title: Controlled Access Zones
talking_points: A controlled access zone is an area set back from a leading edge where conventional fall protection is infeasible and only authorized workers may enter.
The control line must be set back at least 6 feet from the edge (10 feet when working with overhand bricklaying or precast concrete).
Control lines must be 39-45 inches high, flagged every 6 feet, and supported by stanchions strong enough to prevent displacement.
Only the minimum number of workers necessary may enter the controlled access zone. Everyone inside must be trained on the specific procedures.
A controlled access zone is not the same as a warning line and is not a license to work unprotected — it is a last resort when other methods won't work.
discussion_prompt: Is the controlled access zone properly set up today — line height, flags, distance from the edge — and who is authorized to enter?

title: Hole Covers and Skylight Protection
talking_points: All floor holes and skylights through which a worker could fall must be guarded with a cover or guardrail system.
Covers must support at least twice the maximum intended load — including the heaviest worker plus any tools or materials they carry.
Covers must be secured against displacement by nails, screws, bolts, or other fasteners. A loose cover is nearly as dangerous as no cover.
Mark covers clearly in a contrasting color with 'HOLE' or 'COVER.' An unmarked cover may be moved by someone who doesn't know what's underneath.
Skylights are particularly dangerous because they look solid but cannot support a person's weight. Use skylight screens or guardrails rated for the load.
discussion_prompt: Are all floor openings and skylights in our work area covered and secured — or do we need to address any before starting work?

title: Drug and Alcohol Awareness on Jobsites
talking_points: Impairment from drugs or alcohol dramatically increases the risk of injury — to yourself and to everyone around you. Most companies have a zero-tolerance policy.
Prescription medications can also cause impairment. If your medication warns against operating heavy equipment or causes drowsiness, notify your supervisor before starting work.
If you suspect a co-worker is impaired, say something. This is not about getting someone in trouble — it is about keeping everyone alive.
Workers who hold a commercial driver's license (CDL) are subject to DOT drug and alcohol testing requirements, including random, post-accident, and reasonable-suspicion testing.
Employee assistance programs (EAPs) are confidential resources. If you or someone you know needs help, reach out — it's a sign of strength, not weakness.
discussion_prompt: Does everyone know how to access the company's EAP — and do you feel comfortable using it if needed?

title: Fatigue Management — Shift Work and Overtime
talking_points: Fatigue impairs judgment, reaction time, and coordination — similar to the effects of alcohol. After 17 hours awake, performance equals a 0.05% blood alcohol level.
The risk of workplace accidents doubles after 12 hours of work. After 16 hours, it triples.
If you are fatigued, speak up. Pushing through is not toughness — it is a risk to yourself and your crew.
Hydration, nutrition, and quality sleep are the foundation of fatigue management. Energy drinks and caffeine mask fatigue but do not eliminate the risk.
Supervisors: monitor your crew for signs of fatigue — slow reactions, confusion, irritability, and near-misses. Adjust schedules and tasks accordingly.
discussion_prompt: Is anyone on the crew running on less than 5 hours of sleep — and what can we do to manage the risk today?

title: Mental Health and Suicide Prevention in Construction
talking_points: Construction has the highest suicide rate of any industry. This is a safety issue — it belongs in our toolbox talks alongside falls and electrocution.
Risk factors in our industry include physical pain, long hours, time away from family, job insecurity, and a culture that discourages talking about struggles.
Watch for warning signs in your crew: withdrawal, hopelessness, giving away possessions, increased substance use, talking about being a burden, or drastic mood changes.
If you're concerned about someone, ask directly: 'Are you thinking about hurting yourself?' Asking does not plant the idea — it opens the door to help.
The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is available 24/7 by calling or texting 988. Your company's EAP is another confidential resource.
discussion_prompt: Does everyone know how to reach the 988 Lifeline and our company's EAP — and would you feel comfortable reaching out if you needed to?

title: Permit-to-Work Systems
talking_points: High-hazard activities — confined space entry, hot work, excavation, lockout/tagout, and work on energized equipment — require a written permit before work begins.
A permit documents the hazards, the controls in place, the workers involved, and the duration of the authorization. It is a communication tool, not just paperwork.
Permits are time-limited and area-specific. A permit from yesterday does not cover today's work — even if the task is the same.
The permit must be signed by an authorized person and posted at the work location. All workers involved must read and understand the permit.
When the work is complete, the permit must be closed out and returned. Review any issues or near-misses that occurred during the work.
discussion_prompt: Do we have all required permits in place for today's work — confined space, hot work, excavation — and are they posted?

title: Multi-Employer Worksite Responsibilities
talking_points: On multi-employer construction sites, OSHA can cite four types of employers: the creating employer (who caused the hazard), the exposing employer (whose workers are exposed), the correcting employer (who is responsible for fixing it), and the controlling employer (who has general authority over the site).
The general contractor is typically the controlling employer and has the broadest responsibility for site safety — even for subcontractor activities.
If you see a hazard created by another trade, do not assume it is 'not your problem.' Report it to your supervisor and to the GC's safety team.
Subcontractors must comply with OSHA standards and the GC's site safety plan. Having your own safety program does not exempt you from site-specific rules.
Pre-task planning meetings with multiple trades help identify conflicts — like one crew cutting above another crew's work area.
discussion_prompt: Are there any multi-trade conflicts today — different crews working above, below, or adjacent to each other — that we need to coordinate?

title: Toolbox Talk Best Practices (Meta)
talking_points: An effective toolbox talk is relevant to the day's work. If you're pouring concrete today, talk about formwork safety — not confined spaces.
Keep it to 5-10 minutes. Be concise, practical, and conversational. This is a discussion, not a lecture.
Ask questions and encourage participation. A crew that talks about safety together watches out for each other.
Document attendance with signatures and keep records. This is both a compliance requirement and evidence of your commitment to training.
Follow up during the day. If the morning talk was about ladder safety, check ladders in the afternoon. Consistency between words and actions is what builds a safety culture.
discussion_prompt: What safety topic would YOU want to cover in a toolbox talk this week — what's on your mind?

title: Incident Investigation and Near-Miss Reporting
talking_points: Fatalities must be reported to OSHA within 8 hours. Amputations, loss of an eye, or inpatient hospitalization must be reported within 24 hours.
Incident investigation is not about assigning blame — it is about identifying root causes and preventing recurrence.
Near-misses are free lessons. A near-miss today is tomorrow's injury if we don't address the root cause. Report every one.
Use a structured investigation method: what happened, why it happened (ask 'why' five times), what conditions allowed it, and what we will change.
Share investigation findings with the entire team. Lessons learned in private benefit no one.
discussion_prompt: Has anyone had a near-miss recently that we should discuss — even if it seemed minor at the time?

title: OSHA Recordkeeping (300/300A/301)
talking_points: The OSHA 300 Log records every work-related injury and illness that meets the recording criteria — medical treatment beyond first aid, days away from work, restricted duty, or loss of consciousness.
The 300A Summary must be posted in the workplace from February 1 through April 30 each year, where all employees can see it.
Employers with 250 or more employees, or those in certain high-hazard NAICS codes, must electronically submit 300, 300A, and 301 data to OSHA.
All records must be maintained for at least 5 years. They must be available for inspection by OSHA, employees, and employee representatives.
Accurate recordkeeping is not just about compliance — it identifies trends that help you target your safety efforts where they will have the most impact.
discussion_prompt: Do you know where the OSHA 300A Summary is posted at our site — and have you looked at it this year?

title: Scaffolding — Rolling/Mobile Scaffolds
talking_points: All caster wheels must be locked before anyone climbs or works on a mobile scaffold. Unlocked casters are one of the most common scaffold citation items.
The maximum height of a mobile scaffold must not exceed four times the minimum base dimension — unless outriggers are used to widen the base.
No workers may ride on a mobile scaffold while it is being moved. Everyone must dismount before repositioning.
Move the scaffold on a level surface only. Even a slight grade can cause a mobile scaffold to roll uncontrollably.
Apply the same guardrail and platform requirements as supported scaffolds — top rail, midrail, toeboards, and full planking.
discussion_prompt: Are the casters locked on our rolling scaffold right now — and is the height within the 4:1 ratio?

title: Drywall and Interior Finishing Hazards
talking_points: Drywall stilts increase fall risk — maintain balance, avoid uneven surfaces, and never use stilts on scaffolding (it is prohibited).
Joint compound and drywall sanding generate fine dust. Some older joint compounds may contain silica. Use a HEPA vacuum sander or wet sanding methods and wear respiratory protection.
Full sheets of drywall are heavy and awkward. Use a drywall lift for ceiling installations and team-lift for wall panels when possible.
Utility knives are the most common source of cuts in drywall work. Use a retractable blade, cut away from your body, and replace dull blades — they require more force and slip more easily.
Poor lighting in unfinished spaces increases tripping hazards and strains your eyes. Set up temporary task lighting before starting finish work.
discussion_prompt: Is anyone using stilts today — and are they on a level, clear surface away from openings?

title: Painting and Coatings — Chemical Exposure
talking_points: Spray painting requires ventilation to control overspray and fume exposure. In spray booths, airflow must draw fumes away from the painter's breathing zone.
Solvent-based coatings produce flammable vapors — monitor LEL levels and ensure no ignition sources are present in the spray area.
Check the SDS for each coating you are using. The SDS specifies the correct respiratory protection, glove type, and ventilation requirements.
Two-component coatings (epoxies, polyurethanes) often contain isocyanates, which are potent respiratory sensitizers. Once sensitized, even tiny exposures cause asthma attacks.
Lead-based paint may be present on older structures being repainted. Test before disturbing and follow lead-safe work practices if lead is confirmed.
discussion_prompt: What coatings are we applying today, and have we checked the SDS for respiratory and ventilation requirements?

title: Masonry Wall Bracing
talking_points: Masonry walls over 8 feet in height must be braced to prevent collapse until permanent structural support is in place.
A limited access zone must be established on the unbraced side of the wall equal to the wall height plus 4 feet. No one may enter this zone.
Wind is the most common cause of masonry wall collapse during construction. Monitor conditions and increase bracing in gusty weather.
Braces must be designed or specified by a competent person and attached to both the wall and a stable anchor point.
Do not remove bracing until the mortar has achieved adequate strength and permanent structural connections (roof, floor, cross-walls) are in place.
discussion_prompt: Are the masonry walls in our work area braced — and is the limited access zone established and respected?

title: Precast Concrete Erection
talking_points: Temporary bracing for precast elements must be designed by a Professional Engineer and installed before the crane releases the piece.
Use tag lines to control the load during placement. Never stand between a precast element and a fixed object during positioning.
Inspect all rigging hardware — lifting inserts, coil bolts, anchors — before each lift. Hardware must match the element weight and configuration.
Fall protection is required for erection crews working at height. Plan anchorage points before the pieces are placed, not after.
No workers may be under a suspended precast element at any time. Barricade the drop zone and the swing radius.
discussion_prompt: Has the engineer's bracing plan been reviewed for today's picks — and are all rigging inserts inspected?

title: Temporary Traffic Control (Work Zones)
talking_points: A Temporary Traffic Control (TTC) plan is required for all work that affects public traffic. The plan must conform to the MUTCD and any state or local requirements.
Channelizing devices — cones, barrels, barriers — must be placed per the plan to guide traffic around the work area. Include adequate advance warning signs.
Buffer space between the work area and live traffic must account for speed, stopping distance, and the type of traffic control device used.
Night work requires enhanced delineation — reflective channelizers, flashing lights, and illuminated signs. Standard cones without reflectors are not sufficient at night.
Workers in the TTC zone must wear high-visibility clothing appropriate for the speed and time of day.
discussion_prompt: Is our work zone set up exactly per the TTC plan — and are all the signs and channelizers in the right positions?

title: Utility Locating (Call Before You Dig)
talking_points: Call 811 at least 48-72 hours before any excavation. This is a legal requirement in every state and initiates utility locating.
Utility marks use a standard color code: Red = electric, Yellow = gas/oil, Orange = telecom, Blue = water, Green = sewer, White = proposed excavation.
Hand-dig within 18-24 inches of utility marks (the exact distance varies by state). Mechanical equipment may not be used within this tolerance zone.
Unmarked or unexpected utilities can still be present — especially private utilities not registered with 811. Use caution and watch for signs of buried lines.
If you strike a utility, stop work immediately, evacuate the area, and call 911 and the utility company. Do not attempt to repair a damaged gas or electrical line.
discussion_prompt: Has 811 been called for today's dig — and do we have the utility locate ticket number posted?

title: Dewatering and Pumping Operations
talking_points: Water accumulation in excavations must be controlled continuously. Standing water weakens trench walls and can trigger sudden cave-ins.
Dewatering pumps must be sized for the expected inflow. A pump that cannot keep up creates a false sense of security while water undermines the soil.
Electrical equipment near water creates an electrocution hazard. Use GFCI protection on all pumps and power equipment in wet areas.
Discharge water must be directed away from the excavation and away from other work areas. Check environmental permits for discharge requirements.
If water is rising faster than it can be controlled, evacuate the excavation. Workers should never remain in a trench where water levels are increasing.
discussion_prompt: Is our dewatering system keeping up with the inflow today — and where is the discharge going?

title: Crane Load Charts and Capacity
talking_points: The load chart must be in the cab and readily accessible to the operator at all times. It specifies the rated capacity for every combination of boom length, radius, and configuration.
Capacity decreases as the radius increases. A crane rated for 50 tons at 20-foot radius may only be rated for 10 tons at 80 feet — always check the chart.
The total load includes the weight of the object PLUS the rigging, block, and ball. Forgetting to account for rigging weight has caused overloads.
Use 75% of rated capacity as the planning threshold. This provides a margin for wind, dynamic loading, and measurement uncertainty.
If the LMI (load moment indicator) alarms, stop the lift immediately. Do not override the LMI — it exists to prevent tip-over and structural failure.
discussion_prompt: What is the heaviest pick planned for today — and have we verified it against the load chart for the planned radius?

title: Crane Operator Certification
talking_points: All crane operators must be certified by an accredited certifying body such as NCCCO, CIC, or NCCER. Employer-only certifications are not sufficient.
Certification is type-specific (lattice boom, telescopic, tower) and capacity-specific. An operator certified on a 50-ton telescopic is not certified for a 200-ton lattice.
Certification must be renewed every five years. Medical fitness evaluations are also required — a crane operator must meet specific physical standards.
Employers must also evaluate each operator on the specific equipment they will operate at each jobsite. Certification alone is not enough — site-specific evaluation is required.
Trainees may operate cranes only under the direct supervision of a certified operator, and the trainee must be in the process of obtaining certification.
discussion_prompt: Is our crane operator's certification current, and does it cover the specific type and capacity of the crane on site?

title: Ladder Safety — Step Ladders
talking_points: Open the stepladder fully until the spreaders lock. A partially opened stepladder is inherently unstable and can collapse without warning.
Never stand on the top cap or the top step of a stepladder. These positions create a high center of gravity with no support to hold onto.
Place the ladder on a firm, level surface. If the floor is uneven, find a better location — do not use shims, boards, or bricks to level the ladder.
Follow the duty rating: Type IA (300 lbs, industrial) is the minimum for most construction work. Type II (225 lbs, commercial) may not be sufficient for a worker plus tools.
Do not overreach — your belt buckle should stay between the side rails. If you can't reach, move the ladder.
discussion_prompt: Is the stepladder you used last time the correct duty rating for your weight plus your tools?

title: Signs, Signals, and Barricades
talking_points: DANGER signs (red, black, and white) indicate an immediate hazard that could cause death or serious injury. Do not enter a danger zone without authorization.
CAUTION signs (yellow with black text) warn of potential hazards that could cause moderate injury. Follow the instructions on the sign.
Color coding follows ANSI Z535: Red = danger/fire, Orange = warning, Yellow = caution, Green = safety/first aid, Blue = information.
Barricade tape is for awareness only — it is not a physical barrier. Respecting tape boundaries requires a conscious decision by every worker who sees it.
When you set up a barricade, make sure it is visible, complete (no gaps), and communicated to the crew. A barricade that nobody knows about protects nobody.
discussion_prompt: Is every barricade and sign on our site today still in place and properly communicated — or have any been knocked down or ignored?

title: Personal Hygiene — Hazardous Materials
talking_points: Never eat, drink, smoke, or apply cosmetics in areas where hazardous materials are present. Ingestion is a real exposure route — contaminated hands transfer chemicals to food.
Wash your hands and face with soap and water before eating, drinking, or leaving the work area. Hand sanitizer does not remove heavy metals or chemical residues.
Change out of contaminated clothing before leaving the site. Clothes contaminated with lead, silica, or asbestos can expose your family at home.
Decontamination stations must be provided when working with particularly hazardous substances — lead, asbestos, and certain chemicals.
Shower facilities may be required depending on the substance. Check the SDS and the applicable OSHA standard for hygiene requirements.
discussion_prompt: Are we washing up before breaks — and are we changing clothes before going home when we've been working with dusty or chemical materials?

title: Struck-By Prevention — Falling Objects
talking_points: Toeboards on scaffold platforms prevent tools and materials from being kicked off the edge. They must be at least 3.5 inches high.
Overhead canopies or covered walkways are required when workers must pass under areas where there is a risk of falling objects.
Use tool lanyards for all hand tools when working at height. A dropped wrench from 100 feet can strike with the force of a bullet.
Debris nets below active work areas catch falling material. They must be inspected regularly and cleared of accumulated debris.
Hard hat zones must be established and enforced wherever there is any risk of falling objects — even in areas that seem low-risk.
discussion_prompt: Is everyone working at height today using tool lanyards — and is the area below barricaded or protected?

title: Excavation — Soil Classification (Hands-On)
talking_points: The competent person must classify soil as Type A (most stable), Type B, Type C (least stable), or stable rock. Classification determines the required protective system.
Visual tests: look for cracks or fissures in the excavation walls, water seepage, layers of sand or gravel, evidence of previous backfill, and signs of vibration damage.
Thumb penetration test: if you can easily press your thumb into the soil, it is likely Type C. If it takes considerable pressure, it may be Type A or B.
The pocket penetrometer provides a quantitative reading. Type A requires unconfined compressive strength above 1.5 tsf; Type B is 0.5-1.5 tsf; Type C is below 0.5 tsf.
If any condition suggests the soil is weaker than initially classified — water seepage, vibration, recent rain, or mixed soil layers — reclassify to the weaker type.
discussion_prompt: What type of soil are we working in today — and how was it classified? Can the competent person walk us through the test they performed?

title: Concrete Saw Safety (Walk-Behind and Handheld)
talking_points: Use the blade guard at all times — never remove it for a deeper cut or to improve visibility. The guard protects against blade contact and flying debris.
Wet cutting is the primary silica dust control for concrete saws. The water supply must be connected and flowing before you begin cutting.
Check the blade RPM rating — it must match or exceed the saw's operating speed. A blade rated below the saw's RPM can disintegrate during use.
Maintain firm footing and a stable stance. Walk-behind saws can kick or pull if they encounter rebar or an uneven surface.
Respiratory protection (minimum APF 10, such as an N95) is required in addition to wet cutting when dust is visible or when conditions prevent effective water delivery.
discussion_prompt: Is the water supply connected to our concrete saw right now — and is the blade the correct rating for this saw?
